seo_description: Prepare thoughtful questions to ask the interviewer: team, success, growth and culture, plus questions to avoid and how to tailor them to each interview round.
content:
When an interviewer asks, "Do you have any questions for us?", the best answer is yes: ask two or three thoughtful, role-specific questions about the work, the team and how success is measured. Good questions show that you have researched the company, that you are serious, and that you are evaluating the job as carefully as they are evaluating you.

The interview is a two-way conversation. You will spend a large part of your week in this job, so you deserve real answers before you accept it.

## Why your questions matter

Your questions do three things at once:

1. They show curiosity and preparation.
2. They give you information to decide whether the job fits you.
3. They leave a final impression, since this is often the last part of the interview.

Weak or missing questions waste that opportunity. Strong questions can shift the conversation from interrogation to discussion.

## Questions about the role

- "What would a typical week look like in this position?"
- "What are the most important things to accomplish in the first three to six months?"
- "What does success look like in this role, and how is it measured?"
- "What are the biggest challenges someone in this position would face?"

These reveal what you will actually be doing, which can differ from the job posting.

## Questions about the team and manager

- "How is the team structured, and who would I work with most closely?"
- "How does the team usually communicate and make decisions?"
- "How would you describe your management style?"
- "How is feedback usually given?"

If you are speaking with a future manager, the third question is especially helpful. Listen for specifics rather than buzzwords.

## Questions about growth and development

- "What opportunities for learning or training are available?"
- "How have people in this role grown within the company?"
- "How are goals and performance reviewed?"

These show ambition. They also help you judge whether the company invests in people.

## Questions about the company and its direction

- "What are the main priorities for the team over the next year?"
- "How does this team contribute to the company's larger goals?"
- "What do you enjoy most about working here?"

The last question is gentle and often produces honest answers. Pay attention to hesitation.

## Questions about process

- "What are the next steps in the hiring process?"
- "Is there anything about my background you would like me to clarify?"

The second question is powerful. It gives you a chance to address a concern before you leave the room.

## Adapt questions to the interview stage

- **Recruiter or screening call:** Ask about the process, timeline and the role's general scope.
- **Hiring manager interview:** Ask about expectations, team goals and management style.
- **Team or peer interview:** Ask about day-to-day work, collaboration and culture.
- **Senior or final interview:** Ask about strategy, priorities and how the role may evolve.

## How to prepare questions with AI

AI can help brainstorm, but your research should shape the final list.

> I am interviewing for [job title] at [company type or name]. Here is the job description: [paste]. Suggest ten thoughtful questions I could ask the interviewer, grouped by role, team, growth and company. Avoid generic questions that could apply to any company and avoid questions about salary or vacation.

Then check official company pages or recent public announcements to make two or three questions specific. Be careful to verify any facts instead of assuming a tool is correct.

## Listen and follow up

Do not treat your questions as a checklist. If an answer opens a new topic, follow it with "Could you tell me more about that?" Real conversation is more memorable than a prepared list. Jot down notes after the interview, since the answers will also help you write your thank-you message.

## Questions to avoid

- **Anything easily answered by the website.** It signals lack of research.
- **"What does your company do?"** See above.
- **Only about perks.** Questions about holidays and benefits alone suggest you care more about what you get than what you give. These are fine later, but not as the sole focus.
- **Negative or confrontational questions.** Avoid anything that sounds like an accusation.
- **Questions that put the interviewer on the spot** about confidential matters like other employees or private finances.

## Reading the answers

The answers you receive are data about the job. Notice whether the interviewer gives specific examples or speaks in vague generalities. Notice whether different interviewers describe the role in similar ways, since mismatched answers may signal unclear expectations. If someone hesitates when you ask about workload or turnover, make a note and consider asking another team member in a later round.

### Questions for remote or hybrid roles
If the position is remote or hybrid, ask how the team handles time zones, how work is documented, how often people meet in person if at all, and what tools the team uses for communication. These details shape daily life far more than a job title.

### Questions for early-career candidates
If you are applying for your first role, consider asking about mentoring, onboarding and how new team members are supported in their first weeks. Employers value candidates who think about learning, and you gain insight into how welcoming the environment is.

### Closing the interview well
Once your questions are answered, close with a short summary: thank the interviewer, restate in one sentence why the role excites you and how your background fits, and confirm the timeline. This final minute leaves a clear, confident impression and shows you listened throughout the conversation.

## Common mistakes

- **Having no questions.** It may look like disinterest.
- **Asking too many.** Respect the time limit.
- **Asking the same questions of every interviewer.** In a multi-round process, vary them to learn from different people.
- **Ignoring the answers.** Show that you listened.
- **Delaying the question about next steps.** Always leave knowing the timeline.
- **Being too generic.** "What is the culture like?" is weak; "How does the team handle disagreements about priorities?" is stronger.

## A short list to copy

```
1. What would success look like in this role after six months?
2. What is the biggest challenge the team is facing right now?
3. How does the team collaborate and share feedback?
4. What opportunities are there to learn and grow here?
5. What are the next steps, and when can I expect to hear back?
```

## Next steps

Write five questions tailored to your next interview, and rank them by importance. Then rehearse your closing with prompts from the [careers prompt library](/prompts/category/careers) and prepare your [follow-up email](/blog) so you can send it within a day. If you also need a polished application, use the [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder).

faq.q: How many questions should I ask at the end of an interview?
faq.a: Prepare three to five, and expect to ask two or three depending on time. Having extras is useful because some may be answered during the conversation. Choose the ones that matter most to your decision.

faq.q: Is it bad to say I have no questions?
faq.a: It can come across as low interest. If the interviewer covered everything, say so, then ask a closing question such as what the next steps are or what a successful first few months looks like.

faq.q: Can I ask about salary and benefits?
faq.a: Yes, but timing matters. Unless the interviewer raises it, wait until you have a clear picture of the role or an offer stage. Early rounds are better for understanding the work and expectations.

faq.q: Should I write my questions down?
faq.a: Yes. Bringing a notebook or a short list is perfectly acceptable and shows preparation. Just listen actively during the answers instead of reading from the page. Taking brief notes on their answers also helps when you write your thank-you message.

title: LinkedIn Profile Optimization: A Step-by-Step Guide
excerpt: Improve your LinkedIn headline, About section, experience and skills so recruiters can find you and understand your value, with templates you can adapt today.
seo_title: LinkedIn Profile Optimization: Step-by-Step Guide
seo_description: Optimize your LinkedIn profile section by section: headline, About, experience, skills and photo, with copy-ready templates and mistakes that hurt visibility.
content:
A strong LinkedIn profile does two jobs: it helps recruiters find you through search, and it convinces them to contact you once they arrive. To optimize it, make your headline specific, write an About section that leads with value, describe experience with results, and fill your skills with the keywords employers use.

LinkedIn works differently from a resume. A resume is a targeted document you send to one employer. A profile is a public page that must work for many readers at once, from recruiters to future colleagues. Treat it as your professional landing page.

## Start with your goal

Before you edit anything, decide what you want the profile to do. Are you looking for a first job, a career change, freelance clients or a promotion? Your answer determines which keywords, projects and tone to emphasize. Write one sentence: "I want to be considered for [type of role] in [industry or location]." Keep it in front of you while you edit.

## Step 1: Write a keyword-rich headline

Your headline appears beside your name in search results, comments and messages, so it carries a lot of weight. The default (your current job title) is often too narrow. Use this pattern:

```
[Target role or current role] | [2-3 key skills or tools] | [short value statement]
```

Examples:

- Content Marketing Associate | SEO, Email, Copywriting | Helping small brands explain what they do clearly
- Final-Year Engineering Student | Python, Automation, IoT | Seeking internships in embedded systems
- Customer Success Manager | Onboarding, Retention, SaaS | Turning new users into confident customers

Use words that real people search for. Look at job postings for your target role and note repeated terms.

## Step 2: Add a clear photo and banner

Use a recent, well-lit photo where your face is clearly visible. Wear what you would wear to an interview in your field. The banner image is optional, but it is free space: use a simple design or a relevant image rather than leaving the default.

## Step 3: Write an About section that leads with value

The first two or three lines matter most because they appear before the "see more" cut. Open with who you help and what you do, not with "I am a motivated professional."

Use this structure:

1. **Hook:** What you do and for whom
2. **Proof:** Two or three achievements, skills or projects
3. **Approach:** How you work or what you care about
4. **Call to action:** What you want readers to do, such as connect or email

Template:

```
I help [audience] [achieve result] through [skills or methods].

Over the past [time], I have [achievement 1], [achievement 2], and [achievement 3].

I enjoy [type of work] and care about [value, such as clarity, quality or learning].

I'm currently open to [type of roles or collaborations]. You can reach me at [contact preference].
```

Write in the first person and keep the tone natural. Avoid buzzword piles such as "dynamic, results-driven, synergistic."

## Step 4: Rewrite your Experience section

For each role, add two to five bullet points beginning with action verbs. Focus on what changed because of your work, not only on your duties. If you lack paid experience, include internships, volunteering, projects and leadership roles in clubs.

Compare:

- Weak: "Responsible for social media."
- Stronger: "Planned and posted weekly content for the club's accounts, growing engagement through consistent formats and clearer captions."

Only claim what is true. Add numbers when you have them, but never invent figures.

## Step 5: Build a targeted skills list

Add your most relevant skills, up to the platform's limit, and put the three or four most important first. Choose skills that match job postings. Ask colleagues, classmates or managers to endorse or recommend you only if they genuinely know your work. A few specific recommendations are worth more than many generic ones.

## Step 6: Use the Featured section and projects

Pin items that show proof: a portfolio, a presentation, an article, a case study or a project. If you are early in your career, a clear project description can be the strongest part of your profile. Add links, short descriptions and your role in each project.

## Step 7: Set your preferences and visibility

Review your settings so recruiters can find you if you are job hunting. Use the available options for signaling that you are open to work, and think about whether you want that visible to everyone or only to recruiters. Check the platform's current settings, since menus and features change.

## Step 8: Fill the details that help search

- Add your location and industry accurately.
- Customize your profile URL.
- Add education, certificates and languages.
- Use the same job titles and keywords across sections, naturally.

## Use AI as an editor, not an author

AI can help you tighten wording. Give it your real information.

> Here is my LinkedIn About section: [paste]. I am targeting [role]. Rewrite it in a clear, human tone in under 200 words. Put the strongest value in the first two lines. Do not add achievements or numbers I have not provided, and avoid buzzwords like "passionate" and "dynamic."

Always edit the output so it sounds like you.

## Keep your profile consistent

Your resume, profile and portfolio should tell the same story. Dates, job titles and achievements must match. Recruiters often compare them, and inconsistencies raise questions.

## Activity and visibility

A complete profile helps, but activity makes you easier to remember. You do not need to post daily. Commenting thoughtfully on posts in your field, sharing a short lesson from a project, or congratulating a contact on a milestone is enough to keep you visible. Write as you would speak to a colleague, and add a real observation instead of a generic "Great post."

### A simple weekly routine
- Spend ten minutes reading posts from people and companies in your target field.
- Leave one or two useful comments.
- Share one short update each week or two, such as something you built, learned or read.
- Accept relevant connection requests and send a few personal ones.

### Privacy and professionalism
Review what is visible publicly. Remove old posts that do not reflect how you want to be seen professionally, and be careful about sharing confidential details about current or past employers. Your goal is a profile that is warm, accurate and safe to show anyone who might hire you.

## Common mistakes

- **Leaving the headline as a job title only.** You waste a keyword opportunity.
- **Writing an About section that starts with clichés.** Lead with value.
- **Listing duties instead of results.** Show impact.
- **Using a blurry or unprofessional photo.** First impressions count.
- **Ignoring the profile after setup.** Update it as you grow.
- **Overstating experience.** Exaggerations are easy to spot and hard to recover from.
- **Not customizing connection requests.** See our guide to networking messages.

## Next steps

Update your headline and the first three lines of your About section today, then work down the page. Make sure your resume matches by using the [resume builder](/resume-builder) and checking it with the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker). For more prompts to refine your profile text, browse the [careers prompts](/prompts/category/careers).

faq.q: What should my LinkedIn headline say?
faq.a: Combine your target role, your key skills or specialty, and a short value statement. For example, 'Junior Data Analyst | SQL, Excel, Dashboards | Turning messy data into clear decisions.' Avoid vague words like 'seeker' or 'enthusiast' alone.

faq.q: How long should my LinkedIn About section be?
faq.a: Aim for three to five short paragraphs or about 150 to 250 words. Put the most important information in the first few lines, because readers often see only a preview before clicking to expand.

faq.q: Do I need a professional photo on LinkedIn?
faq.a: A clear, friendly, well-lit headshot with a simple background helps people trust and recognize your profile. It does not need to be a studio photo; a tidy phone picture is usually fine.

faq.q: How often should I update my LinkedIn profile?
faq.a: Review it at least every few months and whenever you finish a project, earn a certificate, or change direction. Small regular updates keep your profile accurate and show you are active.

title: Networking Messages: Templates for LinkedIn and Email
excerpt: Write networking messages people actually answer. Get templates for LinkedIn requests, alumni outreach, follow-ups and thank-you notes, plus tone tips.
seo_title: Networking Messages: LinkedIn and Email Templates
seo_description: Copy-ready networking message templates for LinkedIn connection requests, alumni outreach, referrals and follow-ups, with tips on tone, length and timing.
content:
A good networking message is short, specific and easy to answer. It says who you are, why you chose this person, and makes one small request, such as fifteen minutes of advice or an answer to a single question. Keep it polite and never open by asking for a job.

Many job seekers dread networking because it feels like begging. It helps to reframe it: you are asking people about their work, which most people enjoy discussing. Your task is to make that conversation easy to start.

## The anatomy of a message people answer

Every effective networking message has four parts:

1. **A personal opening:** Why this person? Mention a shared school, a post they wrote, a project, or a mutual connection.
2. **A short introduction:** Who you are in one sentence.
3. **A specific, small ask:** A concrete request, not "Can I pick your brain?"
4. **An easy exit:** Make it comfortable to say no or to reply briefly.

Always check spelling, especially the person's name and company.

## LinkedIn connection request templates

LinkedIn connection notes have a short character limit, so every word counts.

### Shared background
```
Hi [Name], I'm also a [school] alum, currently studying [field]. I enjoyed your post about [topic]. I'd love to connect and follow your work.
```

### Interest in their work
```
Hi [Name], I've been reading about [topic/company], and your experience as a [role] stood out. I'm exploring this field and would be glad to connect.
```

### After an event
```
Hi [Name], great to hear your talk on [topic] at [event]. Your point about [specific idea] was useful. I'd like to stay in touch.
```

## Messages asking for advice

After someone accepts your request, or if you are writing by email, use a slightly longer message.

```
Hi [Name],

I'm [your name], a [student/professional] interested in [field]. I found your profile through [reason] and was interested in your path from [previous role] to [current role].

I'm trying to understand what skills matter most for entry-level [role]. Would you be open to a 15-minute call in the next couple of weeks, or to answering one or two questions by message? I completely understand if you're busy.

Thank you for considering it.

[Name]
```

## Messages to alumni

Alumni connections can be warm even if you have never met.

```
Hi [Name], I'm a current [program] student at [school]. I saw you work in [field] at [company] and would value hearing how you started. Could I ask you two quick questions about your experience? Happy to work around your schedule.
```

## Asking for a referral

Ask for referrals only when the relationship supports it, and make it easy for the person.

```
Hi [Name], I hope you're well. I noticed [company] is hiring a [role]. My background in [skill] and my work on [project] seem like a match. If you feel comfortable, would you be open to referring me or pointing me to the right person? I've attached my resume. Either way, thank you for your time.
```

Never pressure someone. A referral puts their reputation on the line, so they need to feel confident about you.

## Following up

If you do not hear back, one polite follow-up is acceptable.

```
Hi [Name], just a quick note in case my earlier message was buried. I'd still appreciate your advice on [topic] if you have a few minutes. No worries if the timing isn't right.
```

## Thank-you messages after a conversation

Send these within a day or two.

```
Hi [Name], thank you for taking the time to speak with me. Your advice about [specific tip] was very helpful, and I plan to [action you will take]. I'll let you know how it goes.
```

Later, follow up with a short update. People enjoy hearing that their advice worked.

## Tone and timing tips

- **Be specific, not flattering.** Mention one real detail instead of generic praise.
- **Respect time.** Offer short options, such as a call or a few written answers.
- **Send at reasonable hours.** Business hours in their time zone usually work well.
- **Offer something back.** Share an article, a connection or your own perspective when appropriate.
- **Stay in touch lightly.** A congratulation or relevant link every few months keeps a relationship warm.

## Using AI to draft messages

AI can help with wording, but personal details must come from you.

> Draft a short LinkedIn message (under 90 words) to a [role] at [company]. I am a [your background] and I am interested in [reason]. Mention this specific detail from their profile: [detail]. Ask for a 15-minute chat about how they started. Keep the tone polite and natural, and do not use flattery.

Edit the draft so it sounds like you. Messages that sound copied tend to be ignored.

## Track your outreach

Keep a simple list with name, company, date contacted, response and next step. It prevents duplicate messages and helps you follow up on time. Even a spreadsheet works.

## Networking when you feel shy or have no contacts

If you think you have no network, start smaller than you expect. Classmates, former colleagues, teachers, neighbors, club members and friends of family are all part of it. Many people also find it easier to begin online by commenting on posts or joining a professional group before sending direct messages. Warm contact, even a short comment exchange, makes later requests feel natural.

### Make it a long-term habit
Think of networking as a habit, not a one-time campaign. Aim for a small, steady routine such as two thoughtful messages a week. Keep notes about what each person shared so you can refer to it later. When you hear about a job or article that might help someone, pass it on without expecting anything back. Over time, this generosity builds a reputation people remember.

### Etiquette for referrals and introductions
When someone offers to introduce you, make it easy by writing a short summary they can forward. Include who you are, what you are seeking and why the other person might be a good contact. Always thank both people and let them know the outcome.

## Common mistakes

- **Sending the same generic message to everyone.** Recipients notice.
- **Asking for a job right away.** It can feel transactional.
- **Writing too long.** Long messages are less likely to be read.
- **Being vague about the ask.** "Let me know if you have opportunities" is hard to answer.
- **Forgetting to say thank you.** Gratitude builds relationships.
- **Pushing after a no.** Accept it graciously and move on.
- **Contacting only when you need something.** Stay in touch occasionally.

## Next steps

Pick five people in your target field and send each a personalized message using the templates above. Build the profile they will see with our [LinkedIn guide](/blog), and explore more writing prompts in the [careers prompt library](/prompts/category/careers). If you are also preparing applications, the [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder) can help.

faq.q: How long should a networking message be?
faq.a: Keep it short: three to five sentences for a first message. State who you are, why you are contacting them, and make one small, specific request. Short messages are easier to answer and show respect for their time.

faq.q: Is it okay to message strangers on LinkedIn?
faq.a: Yes, if you are polite, specific and not demanding. Mention a genuine reason for contacting them, such as a shared school or interest, and ask for something small like a short conversation or advice.

faq.q: Should I ask for a job in the first message?
faq.a: Usually not. Start by asking for advice or perspective, which is easier to say yes to. Relationships built on curiosity and respect are more likely to lead to referrals and opportunities later.

faq.q: What if no one replies to my message?
faq.a: Many messages go unanswered because people are busy, not because of you. Send one polite follow-up after about a week or two, then move on and contact other people. Do not send repeated reminders.

title: Salary Negotiation Basics: How to Negotiate a Job Offer
excerpt: Learn the basics of negotiating a job offer: researching market value, timing, what to say, what else to negotiate and scripts you can adapt to your situation.
seo_title: Salary Negotiation Basics: How to Negotiate an Offer
seo_description: Learn how to negotiate a job offer: research pay ranges, time the conversation, use calm scripts, weigh benefits and avoid common negotiation mistakes.
content:
To negotiate a job offer, thank the employer, research a realistic pay range, ask for what you want with a calm reason, and then listen. Negotiation is a normal part of hiring, and a respectful request based on evidence seldom hurts your chances. This guide covers the basics so you can approach it with a plan instead of anxiety.

This article is general educational information. Employment practices and laws differ by country and company, so check local rules and the official offer documents.

## Why negotiation matters

Your starting pay and terms often shape your earnings for years, since future increases may build on them. Even if the difference looks small today, it can compound over time. Negotiating also builds a habit of advocating for yourself professionally, which helps later in performance reviews and promotions.

## Step 1: Research your market value

Gather information from several places so you can build a reasonable range:

- Salary information on reputable job sites
- Pay ranges listed in job postings, where available
- Industry or professional association surveys
- Conversations with people in similar roles
- Recruiters, who often know typical ranges

Adjust for location, company size, industry and your own experience. Write down a low, target and high figure. Your target should be defensible, not wishful.

## Step 2: Know your priorities and your limits

Decide in advance:

- **Ideal outcome:** what would make you very happy
- **Acceptable outcome:** what you would take
- **Walk-away point:** the minimum that makes the job unworkable

Think beyond salary. Learning opportunities, flexibility, commute, team and growth potential matter. The best offer is not always the highest number.

## Step 3: Time it well

The strongest time to negotiate is after you receive an offer, because the employer has already decided they want you. Express enthusiasm, thank them, and ask for a little time to review. A reasonable request such as "Could I get back to you by Thursday?" is usually fine.

If you are asked about salary expectations earlier, you can respond with a researched range, or say, "I would like to learn more about the role and responsibilities first. Could you share the range budgeted for this position?" Some places also restrict asking about pay history, so check local rules.

## Step 4: Make the ask

Be warm, clear and specific. Start with appreciation, state your request, and give a reason connected to value or market data.

### Script: asking for a higher salary
```
Thank you so much for the offer. I'm excited about the role and the team. Based on my research on similar positions and the skills I'd bring in [skills/experience], I was hoping for a salary closer to [figure]. Is there flexibility to adjust the offer?
```

### Script: when the employer says the budget is fixed
```
I understand the salary range is set. Would there be flexibility in other areas, such as a signing bonus, an earlier salary review in six months, or additional learning support?
```

### Script: asking for time
```
Thank you for the offer. I would like to review the details carefully. Could I respond by [date]?
```

Then stop talking. Silence is part of negotiating, and filling it often leads to hasty concessions.

## What else you can negotiate

If the base pay cannot move, look at the package:

- Start date
- Signing or relocation bonus
- Performance bonus structure
- Remote or flexible schedule
- Extra paid leave
- Professional development or certification funding
- Title or scope of responsibility
- Review timeline and growth path

Ask for the details in writing and read the full offer, including probation periods and notice terms.

## Handling the response

Employers may respond in several ways:

- **They agree.** Confirm the new terms in writing before accepting.
- **They counter with a smaller increase.** Decide whether it meets your acceptable range.
- **They say no.** Ask if there is any other flexibility, and make your decision based on the whole offer.
- **They need time.** Be patient and stay polite.

Never accept or reject under pressure. You are allowed to ask for time to decide.

## Preparing with AI

AI tools can help you rehearse scripts, but they cannot know your market, so verify figures with real sources.

> Act as a hiring manager. I received an offer for [role] at [type of company]. I want to ask for a higher salary because [reasons]. Role-play a negotiation with me. Push back politely with common objections like budget limits, and give me feedback on my tone and clarity after each reply.

Use the practice to find phrases you are comfortable saying aloud.

## Mindset

Think of the conversation as collaboration, not conflict. You and the employer both want a good long-term fit. Be enthusiastic, flexible and honest. Avoid ultimatums, and never bluff about competing offers. If you do have another offer, mention it truthfully and politely.

## Negotiating in different situations

### Internal raises and promotions
The same principles apply when you ask for a raise. Keep a record of achievements, feedback and added responsibilities, and compare your pay to market data for your role. Request a meeting rather than raising it casually, explain the value you have delivered, and ask what is needed to reach your target. If the answer is no for now, ask for a clear timeline or goals for a future review.

### Entry-level offers
If you are new to the workforce, you may feel you have no leverage. You still have options. Ask whether the range has any room based on your skills, projects or internships, and consider asking about learning budgets, mentoring or a six-month review. Employers often respond well to candidates who are professional and prepared.

### Staying gracious
Whatever the outcome, thank the person for their time. Employers remember courteous candidates and employees. If you accept, confirm details in writing and begin your new role with a positive tone. If you decline, do it respectfully and leave the door open for future opportunities.

## Common mistakes

- **Not negotiating at all.** Many people accept the first offer out of fear.
- **Giving a number without research.** Make your figure defensible.
- **Making it personal.** Justify requests with skills and market data, not personal expenses.
- **Negotiating by email only when a call would help.** Tone is easier to convey in conversation.
- **Lying.** Dishonesty can end the relationship.
- **Focusing only on salary.** Consider the full package.
- **Accepting verbally and negotiating later.** Settle terms before you say yes.
- **Burning bridges after a no.** You may work with these people.

## Next steps

Write down your range, priorities and two scripts you could use. Practice them aloud. Strengthen your case by documenting your achievements with the [resume builder](/resume-builder), and explore more preparation ideas in the [careers prompts](/prompts/category/careers). For more job-search guides, visit the [blog](/blog).

faq.q: Is it okay to negotiate a first job offer?
faq.a: Yes, it is common and usually expected to be professional. A polite, well-researched request rarely causes an offer to be withdrawn. Be realistic about your experience and flexible about what you ask for.

faq.q: When should I discuss salary in the hiring process?
faq.a: Ideally after you have an offer or when the employer clearly wants you, because that is when your leverage is strongest. If asked earlier, you can give a researched range or ask about the budget for the role.

faq.q: How do I find out what a fair salary is?
faq.a: Check multiple sources: salary data on job sites, industry reports, professional associations, public pay ranges in postings and conversations with people in the field. Pay varies by location, company size and experience, so compare several sources.

faq.q: What can I negotiate besides salary?
faq.a: Depending on the employer, you might discuss the start date, bonus, remote or flexible work, learning budget, title, extra leave, review timing or relocation support. Choose what matters most to you.

title: Career Change Plan: How to Switch Careers Step by Step
excerpt: A practical step-by-step plan for changing careers: clarify your reasons, map transferable skills, test the field, build proof and tell your story to employers.
seo_title: Career Change Plan: How to Switch Careers Step by Step
seo_description: Plan a career change with confidence: assess your skills, research fields, test with small projects, fill skill gaps and explain your story to hiring managers.
content:
A successful career change usually follows a clear sequence: understand why you want to move, identify which skills transfer, explore the new field, close the biggest gaps with real projects, and then tell a convincing story to employers. You rarely have to start from zero, and a deliberate plan makes the switch less risky and less overwhelming.

Changing careers can feel like a leap, but it is better treated as a series of small experiments. Each step teaches you something and lets you adjust before committing fully.

## Step 1: Clarify why you want to change

Before choosing a destination, understand what you are leaving. Write answers to these questions:

- What parts of my current work do I enjoy, and what drains me?
- Is the problem the role, the manager, the company or the whole field?
- What do I value most: stability, creativity, income, impact, flexibility, learning?
- What would an ideal workday look like?

Sometimes a change of employer or role within your field solves the issue. Other times a full change is the right move. Being honest here saves months of effort.

## Step 2: Inventory your transferable skills

You likely have more relevant skills than you think. List them under three headings:

- **People skills:** communication, teaching, negotiation, leadership, customer service
- **Thinking skills:** analysis, research, planning, problem solving, writing
- **Technical skills:** software, tools, languages, specialized knowledge

Then look at your achievements, not just your duties. A teacher who explains complex ideas, a retail manager who handles scheduling and a nurse who stays calm under pressure all have skills many employers want. Translate your experience into the language of the new field.

## Step 3: Explore and shortlist target fields

Research two or three possible directions rather than one. For each, find out:

- What do people in this field actually do day to day?
- What skills and tools are commonly required?
- What entry points exist for career changers?
- How does the job market look in your region? Check job postings and official labor information.

Read many job descriptions and note repeated requirements. They show you what employers really need.

## Step 4: Talk to people in the field

Informational conversations are the fastest way to learn what a job feels like. Ask people about their path, daily work and what they wish they had known. Our guide on informational interviews explains how to do this respectfully. Ask: "If you were hiring someone like me, what would convince you?"

## Step 5: Test before you commit

Run small experiments to check your interest and ability:

- Take a short course or tutorial
- Complete a small project
- Volunteer or freelance for a few hours
- Shadow someone or attend an industry event
- Do a small part-time or side task in the field

If you enjoy the work and the experiments go well, continue. If not, you have saved yourself from an expensive mistake.

## Step 6: Close the skill gaps

Compare the job requirements with your skill list and prioritize the gaps that matter most. Choose learning methods that produce visible proof, such as portfolio projects, certificates from reputable providers, or contributions to real work. Aim for evidence over credentials alone. Employers like to see that you can do the work.

## Step 7: Build a bridge role if needed

A direct jump may be hard. Consider an adjacent role that uses your current expertise while moving closer to your target, for example a teacher moving into instructional design, or an accountant moving into financial analytics. A bridge role gives you experience and credibility.

## Step 8: Reposition your resume and profile

Rewrite your resume to emphasize transferable achievements and relevant projects. Lead with a headline that points to your new direction, and place relevant skills near the top. Update your LinkedIn profile to match. Use the vocabulary found in target job postings, but only claim what is true.

## Step 9: Tell your career change story

Prepare a concise, positive explanation:

```
For [number] years I worked in [previous field], where I learned [key skill].
I realized I enjoy [aspect] most, so I started [action: course, project, volunteering].
Now I'm looking to bring [transferable strength] to [new role], where I can [contribution].
```

Avoid criticizing your past field. Focus on what you are moving toward.

## Step 10: Plan your finances and timeline

A career change may involve a temporary pay cut or a period of lower income. Think about your savings, obligations and risk tolerance. Consider changing gradually while keeping your current job. This is general information, not financial advice, so speak with a qualified adviser for personal decisions.

## Using AI to plan

> I currently work as a [current role] with skills in [list]. I am interested in moving into [target field]. Compare my skills with typical requirements for entry-level roles in that field, list the top five gaps, and suggest a three-month learning plan with small project ideas. Remind me to verify requirements against real job postings.

Treat the answer as a starting draft, then check it against actual postings and people in the field.

## Handling doubt and setbacks

Career changers often face a period of discomfort: you may feel like a beginner again after being an expert. That feeling is normal and temporary. Track small wins such as a finished course, a first project, a helpful conversation or an interview, so you can see progress even when job offers are slow to arrive.

### Dealing with rejection
You may hear that you lack direct experience. Treat each rejection as information. Ask for feedback when appropriate, identify patterns, and adjust your resume, projects or target roles. Consider widening your search to related titles, smaller organizations or contract and part-time work that can build your record.

### Keeping balance while you transition
If you are working while changing careers, set a realistic weekly schedule, such as a few focused hours for learning and a few for networking. Consistency matters more than intensity. Review your plan monthly: what did you complete, what did you learn, and what should change? A flexible plan helps you stay motivated without burning out.

## Common mistakes

- **Leaving without researching.** Understand the real work first.
- **Focusing only on credentials.** Projects and evidence often matter more.
- **Underestimating your skills.** Transferable skills are valuable.
- **Chasing trends.** A hot field is not necessarily a good fit for you.
- **Going it alone.** Talk to people and ask for advice.
- **Expecting instant results.** Plan for gradual progress.
- **Apologizing in interviews.** Present your change as a deliberate choice.

## Next steps

Start with the transferable skills inventory today, then shortlist two fields to explore. Build a resume focused on your new direction with the [resume builder](/resume-builder) and browse [resume templates](/resume-templates) suited to career changers. Use the [careers prompt collection](/prompts/category/careers) to plan your transition.

faq.q: How do I know if I should change careers?
faq.a: Consider a change if you feel persistently drained, see no growth, or your interests and values have shifted. Before deciding, separate problems with the job, manager or company from problems with the field itself.

faq.q: Can I change careers without going back to school?
faq.a: Often yes, depending on the field. Many roles accept experience, projects, certificates and self-study. Regulated professions may require formal qualifications, so check the requirements for your target role. Short courses and portfolio projects can help bridge gaps.

faq.q: How long does a career change take?
faq.a: It varies widely. Some people move in a few months through an adjacent role; others take a year or more to build skills and a network. Plan in stages and measure progress by milestones, not deadlines alone.

faq.q: How do I explain a career change in an interview?
faq.a: Give a short, positive story: what you did, what you learned, what drew you to the new field, and how your skills transfer. Show evidence of steps you have already taken, such as courses or projects.

title: How to Find an Internship: A Step-by-Step Search Plan
excerpt: Find an internship with a clear plan: define your goals, build a simple application kit, search in the right places, use your network and follow up well.
seo_title: How to Find an Internship: Step-by-Step Search Plan
seo_description: Find an internship with a practical plan: set goals, prepare your resume and profile, use career centers and networking, apply smartly and follow up well.
content:
To find an internship, decide what you want to learn, prepare a tailored resume and profile, search through several channels (school career services, job boards, company pages and your network), apply consistently, and follow up politely. A steady, organized process beats sending hundreds of identical applications.

Internships can be competitive, but they are also designed for people with limited experience. Employers expect you to be a learner, so your attitude, curiosity and basic skills matter more than a long work history.

## Step 1: Define what you want from an internship

Write down your goals:

- Which field or industry do you want to try?
- What skills do you hope to build?
- Do you prefer a small company, a large organization, a nonprofit or a startup?
- Can you work remotely, hybrid or on-site? What is your location range?
- How long and when are you available?

Clear goals help you pick relevant postings and answer the interview question "Why this internship?" with substance.

## Step 2: Build your application kit

Prepare the materials once, then tailor them.

### Resume
Use a clean one-page format. Include education, relevant coursework, projects, volunteering, clubs, part-time jobs and skills. Lead with the most relevant items. Use our [resume builder](/resume-builder) to structure it and the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) to review keyword coverage.

### Cover letter
Write a short, specific letter explaining why you want this internship and what you can contribute. The [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder) can help you start.

### LinkedIn profile
Make sure your headline mentions your field and the type of role you want, such as "Business student | Seeking marketing internship."

### Mini portfolio
If relevant, gather two or three projects with brief descriptions: what you did, what tools you used and what you learned. A simple document or page is enough.

## Step 3: Search in multiple places

Do not rely on a single job board.

- **Your school's career center:** Staff often know about employers who hire students and may offer resume reviews.
- **Professors and department notice boards:** Faculty frequently hear about opportunities early.
- **Job boards and internship sites:** Use filters for "internship" and your field.
- **Company career pages:** Make a list of 20 organizations you like and check their pages regularly.
- **Professional associations and clubs:** Many share opportunities with members.
- **Alumni networks:** Former students are often glad to help.
- **Career fairs and events:** Prepare a short introduction and bring questions.

Be cautious of listings that ask for payment or sensitive information before hiring. Real internships should not charge you to apply.

## Step 4: Use networking

Many opportunities are never advertised widely. Reach out to alumni, family friends, former teachers and professionals in your target field. Use polite, brief messages that ask for advice, not a job. Our networking message templates can help. Often, a conversation leads to "We might have something."

## Step 5: Apply with tailored materials

For each application:

1. Read the posting carefully and note the key skills.
2. Adjust your resume so the most relevant experience appears first.
3. Mention the company by name in your cover letter, with a specific reason.
4. Follow instructions exactly, including file types and deadlines.
5. Save a copy and record the application in a tracker.

Keep a simple spreadsheet with company, role, date applied, contact, status and next action.

## Step 6: Prepare for interviews

Internship interviews usually focus on motivation, learning ability and teamwork. Practice answering:

- Why are you interested in this field?
- Tell me about a project you are proud of.
- Describe a time you worked in a team.
- What do you hope to learn here?

Use the STAR method for experience-based questions, and prepare questions to ask about training, mentoring and typical tasks.

## Step 7: Follow up

Send a thank-you email within a day of each interview. If you do not hear back by the date they gave you, send a short, polite check-in. Persistence with courtesy shows professionalism.

## Step 8: Build experience while you search

If you are not selected right away, keep developing:

- Start a small project related to your field
- Take a short online course and apply it
- Volunteer for a club or nonprofit
- Offer to help a local organization with a defined task
- Contribute to community or open projects where appropriate

These activities give you stories for interviews and strengthen your next application.

## Use AI to organize your search

> I am a [year/major] student looking for a [field] internship in [location or remote]. Based on my skills: [list], suggest ten types of organizations to target, five keywords to use in search, and a weekly plan for applications and networking. Remind me to verify opportunities on official websites.

Always verify companies and postings on official sources.

## Making the most of an internship once you land it

Finding the role is only the first step. Treat it as a chance to learn and build relationships. Ask what success looks like in the first week, take notes, and request feedback early. Volunteer for small tasks and complete them reliably, because trust leads to bigger responsibilities.

### Build proof as you go
Keep a private log of what you work on, what you learn and any results you contribute to. This will make it easy to update your resume and prepare stories for future interviews. Ask for permission before sharing any work publicly, since some materials may be confidential.

### Leave a good impression
In the final weeks, thank your colleagues, ask for feedback, and if appropriate ask your supervisor whether they would be willing to act as a reference or connect with you on LinkedIn. Stay in touch with a short update every few months. Many full-time offers and future recommendations start with a positive internship experience.

### Handling rejection and silence
Most students receive more rejections or no replies than offers, and that is normal. Employers may have limited places, internal candidates or changing budgets. Keep a calm routine: apply, follow up once, and learn from each interview. If you can, ask for feedback politely. Each application sharpens your materials and your answers, and the next one starts from a better place.

## Common mistakes

- **Starting too late.** Many programs recruit well in advance.
- **Sending the same resume everywhere.** Tailor the top third at least.
- **Ignoring small employers.** They may offer broader responsibilities.
- **Skipping networking.** Many chances come through people.
- **Not following instructions.** It can disqualify you quickly.
- **Giving up after a few rejections.** Rejection is common and not a verdict on your potential.
- **Failing to ask questions.** Show curiosity in interviews.

## Next steps

Set your internship goals this week, build your kit and apply to five well-matched roles. Browse the [careers prompts](/prompts/category/careers) for interview practice, and use the [study planner](/study-planner) to balance applications with your coursework.

faq.q: When should I start looking for an internship?
faq.a: Start several months before you want to begin, since many employers recruit early. Use that time to prepare your resume, profile and projects, then apply as postings open and continue searching afterward.

faq.q: How do I get an internship with no experience?
faq.a: Highlight coursework, projects, volunteering, clubs and skills. Build one or two small projects related to your target field, and use networking and your school's career services to find entry-level and beginner-friendly roles.

faq.q: Should I take an unpaid internship?
faq.a: Think carefully. Unpaid roles may be restricted or regulated depending on your country, so check local rules. Consider what you will learn, who you will work with, and whether the experience justifies the time.

faq.q: How many internships should I apply to?
faq.a: Quality matters more than volume. Apply to roles you match well and tailor each application, while keeping a steady pipeline. Many students apply to a few dozen over several weeks, but there is no fixed number.

title: How to Build a Career Portfolio That Gets You Interviews
excerpt: Build a simple career portfolio that proves your skills: what to include, how to write case studies, where to host it and how to use it in applications.
seo_title: How to Build a Career Portfolio That Gets Interviews
seo_description: Build a career portfolio that proves your skills. Learn what to include, how to write short case studies, where to host it and how to use it in applications.
content:
A career portfolio is a small, organized collection of work that proves what your resume only claims. To build one, pick three to six relevant projects, explain each with a short case study (problem, your role, process, result), host it somewhere easy to open, and link it from your resume and LinkedIn profile.

Hiring managers are busy and often skeptical. A resume says you are "skilled in analysis" or "strong at communication," but a portfolio lets them see it. Even a modest portfolio sets you apart because many candidates never prepare one.

## Who needs a portfolio?

Portfolios are not just for designers and photographers. Consider what proof could look like in your field:

- **Writers and marketers:** articles, campaign plans, email sequences
- **Analysts:** dashboards, reports, data cleaning notebooks
- **Developers:** repositories, small apps, documentation
- **Teachers and trainers:** lesson plans, workshop outlines, learning materials
- **Project managers and operations:** process maps, project plans, improvement summaries
- **Students and career changers:** class projects, volunteer work, self-directed experiments

If you can show how you think and what you can produce, you have a portfolio piece.

## Step 1: Choose your target audience

Decide what role you are aiming for, because your portfolio should help that specific reader say yes. Read job descriptions and list the top skills. Then select projects that demonstrate those skills. A portfolio built for a general audience tends to impress no one.

## Step 2: Select your best projects

Choose three to six pieces that show variety and depth. Good candidates:

- Projects with a clear problem and a result
- Work that uses tools or skills mentioned in job postings
- Pieces you are proud to discuss for ten minutes
- Recent work over very old examples

If you lack professional samples, create them. Redesign a confusing form, analyze a public dataset, write a sample marketing plan for a local business idea, or build a small tool that solves a real problem. Label self-initiated work honestly.

## Step 3: Write short case studies

A case study explains the story behind the work. Use this structure for each project:

```
Title: [Project name]
Overview: One or two sentences on what it was and why it mattered.
My role: What you personally did, and who you worked with.
Problem: What needed solving or improving?
Process: Key steps, decisions and tools. Include one obstacle and how you handled it.
Result: What changed? Use numbers only if they are real. Otherwise describe outcomes or feedback.
Lessons: What you learned or would do differently.
Link/Visual: A screenshot, file, document or demo.
```

Keep each case study to 150 to 300 words. The goal is to let a busy reader grasp your skill quickly, and to give them a hook for interview questions.

## Step 4: Show your thinking, not just the final product

Employers hire people who can reason through problems. Include sketches, drafts, early versions, or a short explanation of why you made certain decisions. Mention trade-offs and what you would improve next. This shows maturity and honesty.

## Step 5: Choose a format and host

Pick the simplest format that works for your field:

- **A personal website or one-page site:** Flexible and professional. Many free and low-cost builders exist; check the provider's current features and terms.
- **A shared document or slide deck:** Fast to build and good for early-career candidates.
- **A public repository with clear README files:** Common for technical roles.
- **A portfolio section on a professional network:** Easy for recruiters to find.

Make sure it loads quickly on a phone, has a readable layout, and does not require a login or special software. Include a short About section and clear contact information.

## Step 6: Organize it for skimming

Recruiters may spend a minute or two on a first look. Help them:

- Lead with your strongest project
- Use clear headings and descriptive titles
- Add a one-line summary above each project
- Use visuals where relevant
- Keep text concise and scannable
- Put your contact link and resume download in an obvious place

## Step 7: Use the portfolio actively

A portfolio only works if people see it.

- Add the link to your resume header and LinkedIn Featured section.
- Mention it in cover letters: "I have included a short case study of a similar project here."
- Reference specific pieces in interviews: "I faced something similar in my [project]; may I show you?"
- Include it in networking messages when relevant.

## Respecting confidentiality and ethics

Never publish confidential employer data, client names without permission, or private information about other people. If a project involved a team, credit collaborators and clarify your own contribution. Never present someone else's work as yours. If you used AI tools to help create parts of a project, be open about how, especially if an employer expects disclosure.

## Using AI to polish your case studies

> Here are my notes about a project: [paste facts]. Turn them into a 200-word case study with the headings Overview, My role, Problem, Process, Result and Lessons. Use plain language, keep every fact accurate, and do not invent numbers or tools I did not mention. Point out missing details I should add.

Then verify every claim and add your own voice.

## Keep it fresh

Review your portfolio every few months. Remove weak or outdated pieces, add new work, and check that links still work. A smaller, current portfolio beats a large, stale one. After each new project or job, ask what you can add.

## Example: turning a small project into a strong piece

Imagine you are a business student who analyzed a public dataset about local bike-share trips. A weak entry says, "Analysis of bike data." A strong entry explains the question you asked (which stations run short of bikes in the morning?), the tools you used (spreadsheets and a basic chart), the finding (a clear pattern at a few stations) and a recommendation. You also state the limits: the data covered a short period and could not explain every cause. That honest framing shows judgment, which employers value highly.

### What to do if your work is private
If your best work is confidential, create a sanitized version. Change names, use sample numbers and describe the process rather than the proprietary details. You can also write a short process summary and offer to discuss details in an interview, within what your agreements allow.

### Portfolio for non-visual roles
If your work does not produce files, use writing. A one-page summary of how you improved a process, handled a difficult customer situation or organized an event can still be a portfolio piece. Add a diagram or checklist if it clarifies your thinking.

## Common mistakes

- **Showing everything.** Curate, do not dump.
- **Having no context.** A screenshot with no explanation is hard to evaluate.
- **Hiding your role.** Be clear about what you personally did.
- **Using confidential material.** It can damage your reputation and relationships.
- **Ignoring mobile users.** Many recruiters view links on phones.
- **Leaving broken links.** Test everything before sharing.
- **Making it hard to contact you.** Put your email or contact link in plain sight.
- **Over-designing.** Clarity matters more than decoration.

## Next steps

Choose your first three projects and write a short case study for each this week. Link the portfolio from a clean resume built with the [resume builder](/resume-builder), and review your keywords using the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker). For more career guidance, explore the [careers prompts](/prompts/category/careers).

faq.q: Do I need a portfolio if I am not a designer?
faq.a: A portfolio can help in almost any field. Writers, analysts, marketers, teachers, project managers and developers can all show work samples, case studies or project summaries that prove skills better than a resume line alone.

faq.q: How many projects should a portfolio include?
faq.a: Three to six strong projects are usually enough. Choose quality over quantity, and pick examples relevant to the jobs you want. A few well-explained pieces beat a long list of unfinished or weak items.

faq.q: Where should I host my portfolio?
faq.a: Use a simple personal website, a professional profile platform, a shared document or a public repository, depending on your field. Choose something easy to open, mobile-friendly and not behind a login.

faq.q: Can I include work I did for a previous employer?
faq.a: Only if you have permission and the material is not confidential. You can often describe the project, your role and the results in general terms, or recreate a similar sample using fictional or public data.

title: Interview Thank-You and Follow-Up Email Templates for You
excerpt: Send a thank-you and follow-up email after an interview with confidence. Includes timing advice, templates for each situation and mistakes that cost candidates.
seo_title: Interview Thank-You and Follow-Up Email Templates
seo_description: Write a polished interview thank-you and follow-up email. Get timing tips, templates for panels, silence and rejections, plus common mistakes to avoid.
content:
Send a short thank-you email within 24 hours of your interview, mention one specific thing you discussed, restate why you are a good fit, and close politely. If you have not heard back after the stated timeline, send one brief follow-up. These small messages show professionalism and keep your name in front of decision makers.

A thank-you note will not rescue a poor interview, but it can reinforce a good one and break a tie between similar candidates. It also gives you one more chance to add something you forgot to say.

## What a good thank-you email does

An effective follow-up does four things:

1. **Thanks them** for their time
2. **Personalizes** with a detail from the conversation
3. **Reinforces your fit** with one brief point
4. **Closes warmly** and signals your interest in next steps

Keep it short. The interviewer likely has a full inbox.

## Timing guidelines

- **Thank-you email:** Within 24 hours, ideally the same evening or next morning.
- **First follow-up if silent:** If they gave a decision date, wait until a day or two after it. If they did not, wait about a week.
- **Second follow-up:** One more, about a week later, then move on and focus on other options.
- **Multi-round processes:** Send a thank-you after each round.

## Prepare while you are still in the interview

Take brief notes during or right after the interview: names, topics, concerns the interviewer raised, and phrases they used. Ask for business cards or email addresses, or confirm the best contact at the end. Your notes will make personalization easy.

## Template 1: Standard thank-you

```
Subject: Thank you, [Interviewer Name] – [Job Title] interview

Hi [Name],

Thank you for taking the time to speak with me today about the [Job Title] role. I enjoyed learning more about [specific topic, such as the team's current project].

Our conversation reinforced my interest in the position. My experience in [relevant skill or project] would let me contribute to [specific goal discussed].

Please let me know if I can provide any additional information. I look forward to hearing about the next steps.

Best regards,
[Your name]
[Phone/LinkedIn]
```

## Template 2: Addressing something you missed

If you realize you forgot to mention something or could improve an answer, add a short paragraph.

```
One more point I wanted to mention: when we discussed [topic], I should have added that [brief relevant example]. I think it shows how I would approach [responsibility].
```

Do not use this to make excuses. Keep it brief and useful.

## Template 3: After a panel interview

Send individual messages to each person, personalizing the middle sentence. If you cannot get all emails, thank the recruiter or coordinator and ask them to share your appreciation with the panel.

```
Hi [Name],

Thank you for including me in today's panel conversation. I especially appreciated your question about [topic], and it made me think about [short reflection].

I'm very interested in the role and would welcome the chance to contribute to [team goal].

Kind regards,
[Name]
```

## Template 4: Following up when you have not heard back

```
Subject: Following up – [Job Title] interview

Hi [Name],

I hope you're well. I'm writing to follow up on my interview for the [Job Title] position on [date]. I remain very interested in the role and would be glad to provide anything else you need.

Could you share an update on the timeline for the decision?

Thank you for your time,
[Name]
```

## Template 5: Responding to a rejection

A graceful reply protects your reputation and keeps future doors open.

```
Subject: Thank you

Hi [Name],

Thank you for letting me know, and for the time you spent interviewing me. I enjoyed learning about [company/team]. I'd appreciate any feedback you're able to share, and I'd like to stay in touch for future opportunities.

Best wishes,
[Name]
```

## Template 6: When you have another offer

If you receive an offer elsewhere and still want to be considered, be honest and polite.

```
Hi [Name],

I wanted to let you know that I've received another offer with a response deadline of [date]. [Company] remains my first choice because of [reason]. If possible, could you let me know where I stand in the process?

Thank you for your consideration,
[Name]
```

Use this only when it is true.

## Formatting and tone

- Use a clear subject line that includes the role.
- Address the person by name and spell it correctly.
- Proofread. A typo in a thank-you note undermines the message.
- Use a professional email address and signature.
- Avoid heavy flattery or exaggerated enthusiasm.
- Send from the same email you used in your application.

## A prompt for drafting

> Write a 110-word thank-you email after my interview for [job title]. Details I want included: we discussed [topic 1] and [topic 2]; I want to emphasize my experience with [skill]. Keep the tone professional and warm, and avoid cliches. Do not invent details about the conversation.

Edit the result so it sounds like you and contains only things that actually happened.

## What to do while you wait

Silence is stressful, but do not stop searching. Continue applying, practice for other interviews and note questions you struggled with. Waiting for one answer can freeze your whole search, so keep momentum.

## Writing for different cultures and industries

Norms differ. In some industries, a short and direct email is preferred, while others expect a slightly more formal tone. If you are interviewing across countries, avoid slang and humor that may not translate, and use a clear subject line. When in doubt, mirror the style of the emails you received from the employer, and stay polite and concise.

### Handwritten notes and other channels
A handwritten note can be a nice touch in some settings, but it is slower and may arrive after a decision. Email is the safest default. Use LinkedIn messages only if you have no email address, and keep them brief. Do not text interviewers unless they have clearly invited you to do so.

### Learning from each interview
After sending your note, spend ten minutes writing down which questions went well, which were hard and what you would answer differently. These notes become your best preparation tool for the next interview, and they help you spot patterns in what you need to practice.

## Common mistakes

- **Sending nothing.** It is a missed chance.
- **Sending a generic template.** Add at least one personal detail.
- **Writing too much.** Keep it concise.
- **Following up too often.** Pestering can harm your chances.
- **Including mistakes or the wrong name.** Proofread and double-check.
- **Sounding desperate.** Stay confident and courteous.
- **Using text messages or social media unless invited.** Email is the safe default.

## Next steps

Draft your thank-you template now, so you can adapt it quickly. Practice your interview with the [careers prompt collection](/prompts/category/careers), and make sure your application materials are polished using the [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder) and [resume builder](/resume-builder).

faq.q: How soon should I send a thank-you email after an interview?
faq.a: Send it within 24 hours, ideally the same day or the next morning. A prompt message shows enthusiasm and keeps you fresh in the interviewer's mind, especially if decisions are made quickly.

faq.q: How long should a follow-up email be?
faq.a: Keep it brief: three to five sentences or about 100 to 150 words. Thank the interviewer, mention one specific point from the conversation, restate your interest and fit, and close politely.

faq.q: When should I follow up if I have not heard back?
faq.a: If the interviewer gave a timeline, wait until it passes, then follow up after a day or two. If not, wait about a week. Send one polite message, and another after a further week at most.

faq.q: Should I send a thank-you to every interviewer?
faq.a: Yes, if you have their contact details. Personalize each message by mentioning something from your conversation with that person. If you only have one contact, ask them to pass along your thanks.

title: Remote Job Search Guide: How to Find and Land Remote Work
excerpt: Find genuine remote jobs with a clear search method: where to look, how to spot scams, how to show remote-ready skills and how to interview for remote roles.
seo_title: Remote Job Search Guide: Find and Land Remote Work
seo_description: A practical remote job search guide: where to look, how to avoid scams, which skills employers want, how to tailor applications and ace remote interviews.
content:
To find a good remote job, search specialized and mainstream job boards with remote filters, check company career pages, use your network, tailor your application to show remote-ready skills, and verify every employer to avoid scams. Remote roles attract many applicants, so a focused, well-organized search matters more than applying everywhere.

Remote work has many shapes: fully remote, hybrid, remote within a country, or remote with set time zones. Understanding which type you want will save time.

## Step 1: Define what "remote" means for you

Before searching, clarify your requirements:

- Fully remote or hybrid?
- Which countries or time zones can you work in?
- Are you legally allowed to work for employers in other locations? Employment and tax rules differ by country, so check official guidance.
- What hours are acceptable?
- Do you want full-time, part-time, contract or freelance?
- Do you have the equipment and internet connection needed?

Many postings say "remote" but restrict candidates to certain regions. Read the details carefully.

## Step 2: Know the skills remote employers value

Remote managers cannot watch you work, so they look for evidence of trust. Highlight these abilities:

- **Written communication:** clear emails, updates and documentation
- **Self-management:** planning your day and meeting deadlines without supervision
- **Reliability:** responding promptly and keeping commitments
- **Tool fluency:** chat tools, video meetings, shared documents, task trackers
- **Proactive collaboration:** flagging problems early and sharing progress
- **Problem solving:** figuring things out before asking for help, and asking well when needed

Prepare short examples for each. A group project coordinated across time zones, a volunteering role done online, or a freelance project delivered independently all count.

## Step 3: Where to search

- **Remote-focused job boards:** Many list only distributed roles. Check reviews and each site's terms.
- **General job boards:** Use filters for "remote" and refine by country.
- **Company career pages:** Many companies hire fully remote and post only on their own sites.
- **Professional communities:** Industry groups, forums and newsletters often share openings.
- **Your network:** Ask contacts whether their teams hire remote workers.
- **Freelance platforms:** Useful for building experience, but compare terms and fees carefully.

Create saved searches and job alerts so you can apply early, since remote postings can fill quickly.

## Step 4: Spot and avoid scams

Remote work attracts fake job offers. Be cautious if you see:

- Requests for payment for training, equipment or "processing"
- Offers made without any interview
- Interviews only through text messaging apps
- Vague job descriptions with unusually high pay
- Requests for your bank details or identity documents before a signed contract
- Pressure to act immediately
- Email addresses from free providers pretending to be a big company

Verify the company independently through its official website, and look for consistent information on professional networks. If something feels off, stop and walk away.

## Step 5: Tailor your application

Adjust your resume and cover letter to show remote readiness:

- Add a line in your summary such as "Experienced in collaborating across time zones using shared documents and chat tools."
- List remote tools you have used, if truthful.
- Show outcomes you achieved independently.
- Mention your working environment, time zone and availability.

Keep your resume tidy and ATS-friendly. Use the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) to review keyword matching.

## Step 6: Prepare for a remote interview

Most remote interviews are video calls. Prepare your setup:

- Test your camera, microphone and internet beforehand
- Choose a quiet, well-lit space with a neutral background
- Keep notes nearby but avoid reading from them
- Close unnecessary tabs and silence notifications
- Have a backup plan, such as a phone hotspot

Expect questions like:

- How do you stay organized and motivated when working alone?
- Describe a time you worked with people in different time zones.
- How do you communicate when you are blocked?
- How do you separate work and personal time?

Use the STAR structure for stories, and ask the employer about their communication norms, core hours and how success is measured.

## Step 7: Show your remote work habits

Some employers give small tasks or trial projects. Treat these as a test of communication: confirm instructions, meet deadlines, and send a clear summary of what you did. Be careful with unpaid tasks and avoid providing substantial free work; reasonable short exercises are common, but extended work without a contract is a red flag.

## A prompt for tailoring your search

> I am looking for remote [role] jobs and I am based in [country/time zone]. Based on my skills [list], suggest 10 search phrases, five types of companies that commonly hire remotely, and three examples of remote-ready achievements I could add to my resume if they are true for me. Remind me to verify companies and job posts on official sources.

Always verify any company or opportunity yourself.

## Build your remote reputation

Participate in online communities, share useful work and write short posts about your projects. Over time, this visibility can lead to inbound opportunities. A clear profile and portfolio help employers evaluate you without meeting you in person.

## Setting up a productive remote work environment

Employers often ask about your workspace, so prepare an honest answer. You do not need an expensive setup, but you do need a reliable internet connection, a quiet place to take calls and a routine. Plan your schedule, include breaks, and set boundaries so work does not spread across your whole day.

### Staying visible and connected
Remote workers can feel invisible. Share short progress updates, document decisions, and take part in team conversations. Use written messages that are clear enough to be understood without a follow-up call. Being easy to work with is one of the strongest signals of remote readiness.

### Contract and legal basics
If you work across borders, check how you will be paid, which taxes apply and whether you are an employee or a contractor. Read agreements carefully and, where needed, seek advice from a qualified professional. This article offers general information only, and rules vary by country.

## Common mistakes

- **Applying only to the most visible postings.** Competition is intense.
- **Ignoring time zone requirements.** Check before applying.
- **Falling for scams.** Never pay to get hired.
- **Writing a generic resume.** Show remote-specific strengths.
- **Poor video setup.** Technical problems create a negative impression.
- **Underestimating isolation.** Consider how you will stay connected and healthy.
- **Skipping questions about expectations.** Ask about hours, tools and communication.

## Next steps

Set your remote criteria, build a saved search list and tailor your resume with the [resume builder](/resume-builder). Prepare for video interviews with the [careers prompts](/prompts/category/careers), and plan your applications each week with the [study planner](/study-planner) as a simple scheduling aid.

faq.q: What skills do employers want in remote workers?
faq.a: Employers typically value clear written communication, self-management, reliability, comfort with collaboration tools, and the ability to work independently while keeping others informed. Show these through examples rather than claims. Employers also like to see clear, friendly updates.

faq.q: How can I spot a remote job scam?
faq.a: Warning signs include requests for payment, vague job descriptions, promises of high pay for little work, interviews only by messaging apps, and requests for bank details before a contract. Research the company independently.
