faq.a: They can be, but some employers prefer experience because remote work needs independence. Beginners can improve their chances with internships, projects, strong communication and roles that offer training or structured onboarding.

title: Personal Branding for Professionals: A Practical Guide
excerpt: Build a personal brand that feels authentic: define your value, choose your message, stay consistent across platforms and share your work without feeling pushy.
seo_title: Personal Branding for Professionals: A Practical Guide
seo_description: Build an authentic personal brand: clarify your strengths, craft a positioning statement, stay consistent online and share your work without feeling salesy.
content:
Personal branding is the deliberate shaping of how others see your skills, values and work. To build one that feels authentic, define what you want to be known for, write a short positioning statement, make your online presence consistent, and share real work over time. It is not about self-promotion; it is about making your value easy to find and easy to remember.

Everyone already has a reputation. Your colleagues, classmates and online contacts have formed opinions about you. Branding simply means being intentional instead of leaving the impression to chance.

## Step 1: Understand your strengths and values

Start with honest self-reflection. Answer these questions on paper:

- What do people usually ask me for help with?
- Which tasks give me energy and which drain it?
- What am I better at than most people around me?
- What do I care about in my work: quality, learning, fairness, creativity, efficiency?
- What feedback have I received repeatedly?

Ask three trusted colleagues, friends or teachers to describe you in three words. Patterns reveal the core of your brand. If everyone says "calm, clear, dependable," that is a useful starting point.

## Step 2: Define your audience

A brand speaks to someone. Who do you want to notice you? Recruiters, hiring managers, clients, collaborators, a professional community or future employers? Think about what they need, what worries them, and what they search for. Your brand should answer their needs in your own style.

## Step 3: Write a positioning statement

Boil your brand down to one or two sentences:

```
I help [audience] [achieve result] by [method/skill], with a focus on [value].
```

Examples:

- "I help small teams turn messy data into clear weekly reports, with a focus on simple explanations."
- "I design lesson materials that help beginners learn technical topics without feeling overwhelmed."
- "I coordinate projects so that busy teams know who is doing what and by when."

This is not your slogan. It is a guide that keeps your profile, conversations and projects aligned.

## Step 4: Make your presence consistent

Check what appears when someone searches your name. Then align these elements:

- **Name and photo:** Use the same professional name and a clear image across platforms.
- **Headline and bio:** Reflect your positioning statement.
- **Portfolio or website:** Show real work and contact information.
- **Resume:** Use similar language and the same achievements.
- **Email signature:** Include your role and a link to your profile.

Consistency builds trust. Mixed messages confuse readers.

Also review old public posts and profiles. Remove or privatize anything that conflicts with the image you want to project at work.

## Step 5: Share work and ideas

You do not have to be an expert to share. Content ideas that suit almost anyone:

- A short lesson from a project or mistake
- A summary of something you learned and how you applied it
- A helpful checklist, template or resource
- A before-and-after example of your work
- A thoughtful comment on an industry topic

Start small, perhaps one post every week or two. Write plainly, give context and keep claims honest. The "learning in public" approach works well: describe what you tried, what happened and what you will do next.

## Step 6: Build relationships, not just visibility

A brand grows through people. Comment on others' work with substance, offer help, thank those who help you, and keep in touch. Join professional communities and take part in discussions. Credit sources when you share ideas. Generosity is an effective long-term brand strategy.

## Step 7: Deliver on the promise

Your brand is validated by your actual work. Meet deadlines, communicate clearly and keep your word. A strong reputation is made in daily behavior as much as in public posts. If your online image promises more than you deliver, trust will fade quickly.

## Step 8: Review and refine

Every six months, ask:

- Is my positioning statement still true?
- What work am I proud of that I have not shared?
- What feedback am I hearing?
- Which platforms or habits are worth continuing?

Your brand should evolve as your skills and goals change.

## Using AI as a thinking partner

> Here are my strengths, values and recent projects: [paste]. Help me draft three versions of a one-sentence positioning statement and a 120-word professional bio. Keep them specific and humble, avoiding buzzwords and exaggerated claims. Ask me clarifying questions before you write.

Use the draft as a starting point and make sure every claim reflects reality.

## Branding for introverts and private people

You do not need to be loud. Quiet branding can mean writing thoughtful articles, building useful tools, helping in smaller communities or being exceptionally reliable. Choose channels that fit your personality, and set boundaries about what you share. Privacy and professionalism are compatible.

## A simple 30-day starter plan

If you want a concrete place to begin, use this month-long outline.

1. **Week 1:** Reflect on strengths and gather feedback from three people. Draft your positioning statement.
2. **Week 2:** Update your headline, bio and photo on your main professional profile. Check your search results and clean up old content.
3. **Week 3:** Choose one project to document. Write a short summary of the problem, your approach and what you learned.
4. **Week 4:** Share that summary, comment thoughtfully on a few posts in your field, and message two people you would like to learn from.

### Measuring progress without obsessing over numbers
Instead of counting likes, notice quality signals: people referencing your work, relevant messages from peers, invitations to talk or collaborate, and recruiters mentioning something specific from your profile. These indicate that your brand is communicating what you intend.

### Handling criticism and disagreement online
If you share opinions, expect that some people will disagree. Respond calmly, thank people for perspectives and correct mistakes openly. A professional response to criticism can strengthen your reputation more than a flawless post.

## Common mistakes

- **Copying someone else's persona.** Authenticity is easier to sustain.
- **Overstating your expertise.** Be honest about your level.
- **Posting without a purpose.** Tie content to your positioning.
- **Neglecting consistency.** Mismatched details create doubt.
- **Chasing numbers.** Followers matter less than relevance and trust.
- **Being only self-promotional.** Share and help others.
- **Ignoring your offline reputation.** Reliability is part of the brand.

## Next steps

Write your positioning statement and update your headline today. Then build a matching resume with the [resume builder](/resume-builder), and use the [careers prompts](/prompts/category/careers) for help with your bio and introductions. Browse the [blog](/blog) for more career growth guides.

faq.q: What is personal branding?
faq.a: Personal branding is the impression people have of your skills, values and work. It is shaped by what you do, how you communicate and what you share publicly. You already have one, even if you have not shaped it deliberately.

faq.q: Do I need to be on social media for personal branding?
faq.a: Not necessarily. A tidy professional profile, a portfolio or website, and good in-person reputation can be enough. Social media can amplify your brand, but consistency and quality matter more than posting everywhere.

faq.q: How do I build a brand if I am early in my career?
faq.a: Focus on learning in public: share projects, lessons and what you are exploring. You do not need to be an expert. A clear direction, curiosity and reliable work build credibility over time.

faq.q: Can personal branding feel fake?
faq.a: It can if it is exaggerated. Keep it honest by basing it on real strengths, values and work. Share what you actually do and think. Authenticity is the foundation of a brand people trust.

title: Your First 90 Days in a New Job: A Practical Success Plan
excerpt: Start a new job well with a 30-60-90 day plan: learn the role, build relationships, deliver early wins and set clear expectations with your manager.
seo_title: Your First 90 Days in a New Job: A Practical Plan
seo_description: Use a 30-60-90 day plan to succeed in a new job: learn the culture, build relationships, deliver early wins and agree on goals with your manager.
content:
The best way to start a new job is with a simple plan: spend the first 30 days learning, the next 30 contributing, and the last 30 owning results, while building relationships and agreeing expectations with your manager. You do not need to prove everything at once. Your goal is to become trustworthy, informed and useful.

The first three months set the tone for how colleagues see you and how you see the job. A little structure helps you avoid common new-hire problems such as confusion about priorities, missed expectations and isolation.

## Before day one

If you have time before starting, prepare:

- Reread the job description and your interview notes
- Review the company's website and public materials
- Ask what to bring, who to meet and what to set up
- Plan your commute or remote setup
- Prepare a short introduction about yourself

Keep your tone positive. Do not criticize your previous employer in your new workplace.

## Days 1 to 30: Learn

Your focus is understanding the people, the work and the culture.

### Understand your role
Ask your manager:

- What are the most important priorities for my first month?
- What does success look like at 30, 60 and 90 days?
- How would you like me to communicate progress?
- What is the best way to ask questions: in the moment, in a regular check-in, or in writing?

Write down the answers.

### Meet people
Schedule short conversations with teammates and colleagues in related areas. Ask about their work, what they find challenging, and how you can help. Learn names and roles. Take notes after each conversation.

### Learn how things work
Observe how decisions are made, how meetings run, what tools are used and which unwritten norms exist. Read documentation, past projects and shared files. Ask about terminology you do not know. Questions are expected from new hires, but try to search first and ask in a well-prepared way.

### Win small tasks
Complete assigned work carefully and on time. Early reliability matters more than ambitious plans.

## Days 31 to 60: Contribute

Now that you understand the basics, begin to add value.

- Take ownership of specific tasks or small projects
- Suggest improvements gently, with context and humility
- Ask for feedback on your work and your communication style
- Keep a running list of questions, problems and ideas
- Build relationships with people outside your immediate team

Avoid proposing sweeping changes too quickly. Many processes have reasons you may not yet know. Ask, "Can you help me understand why we do it this way?" before suggesting alternatives.

## Days 61 to 90: Own

By now you should be working with more independence.

- Deliver a visible result, even a small one
- Share progress updates without being asked
- Identify one improvement opportunity and propose a plan
- Review your goals with your manager
- Discuss your development: skills to learn, projects of interest, feedback

At the end of the period, have a conversation with your manager: "What are the next priorities, and what would you like me to focus on over the next quarter?"

## A 30-60-90 template

```
First 30 days - Learn
- Meet [number] key colleagues
- Understand [core tools/processes]
- Complete [onboarding tasks]
- Clarify goals and success measures with my manager

Days 31-60 - Contribute
- Take ownership of [task/project]
- Share one improvement suggestion
- Ask for feedback on [specific area]

Days 61-90 - Own
- Deliver [specific result]
- Present a short progress update
- Agree on goals for the next quarter
```

Share the draft with your manager and adjust it based on their feedback.

## Build good habits early

- **Keep a work log:** Record what you do each day or week. It helps with performance reviews and your resume.
- **Communicate proactively:** Flag problems early and keep stakeholders informed.
- **Manage your energy:** Learning is tiring, so protect sleep and breaks.
- **Take notes:** Write down instructions, names and decisions.
- **Show appreciation:** Thank people who help you.

## Handling common challenges

### Feeling overwhelmed
Make a list of tasks and ask your manager to confirm priorities. You are not expected to know everything.

### Unclear expectations
Ask directly and summarize your understanding in writing: "To confirm, my priorities this week are A, B and C."

### Difficult colleagues
Stay professional, focus on facts, and seek advice from your manager or a mentor if needed.

### Imposter feelings
Many new employees feel this. Remember that you were hired for a reason, and keep a list of small wins to remind yourself.

## Using AI to prepare

> I am starting a new job as [role] at a [type of organization]. Help me draft a 30-60-90 day plan and a list of ten questions to ask my manager in the first week. Keep it general and flexible, and note that I should adjust it to my manager's real priorities.

Use the output as a conversation starter, not a script.

## Working well with your manager

Your manager is your most important relationship in the first months. Learn how they prefer to communicate, how often they want updates and what they care about most. Ask for a regular one-on-one meeting if there is not one already, and arrive with a short agenda: progress, questions and any blockers.

### Managing up respectfully
Bring solutions as well as problems. If something is not working, describe what you have tried, what you think the options are and what you recommend. Managers appreciate employees who make decisions easier.

### Remote and hybrid onboarding
If you start remotely, be extra deliberate about connection. Schedule video chats with teammates, ask where information lives, and confirm which channels to use for urgent and non-urgent matters. Write down what you learn in a personal guide that you can update as you go. It also becomes a useful resource for the next new hire.

## Common mistakes

- **Trying to change everything immediately.** Learn before you suggest.
- **Not asking questions.** Silence can look like confidence but leads to errors.
- **Staying isolated.** Relationships matter for support and opportunities.
- **Ignoring feedback.** Ask for it and act on it.
- **Overpromising.** Commit to what you can deliver.
- **Complaining early.** Be careful about gossip and negativity.
- **Forgetting to document wins.** You will need them later.

## Next steps

Write your own 30-60-90 plan before day one and share it with your manager. Keep your resume updated as you learn using the [resume builder](/resume-builder), and explore the [careers prompts](/prompts/category/careers) for communication scripts. For more growth-focused guidance, visit the [blog](/blog).

faq.q: What should I do in the first week of a new job?
faq.a: Focus on learning: meet your team, understand your responsibilities, set up your tools, and ask your manager about priorities and expectations. Listen more than you talk, and take notes so you remember names and processes.

faq.q: What is a 30-60-90 day plan?
faq.a: It is a simple roadmap for your first three months: the first 30 days for learning, the next 30 for contributing, and the final 30 for owning results. Share it with your manager so goals are clear.

faq.q: How do I make a good impression at a new job?
faq.a: Be reliable, curious and respectful. Arrive prepared, meet commitments, ask thoughtful questions, accept feedback gracefully and show appreciation. Small consistent behaviors build trust faster than trying to impress. Always stay humble and willing to learn.

faq.q: How do I ask for feedback in a new role?
faq.a: Ask your manager early, such as at the end of the first or second week, what is going well and what to improve. Specific questions like 'What would make my work more useful to you?' invite useful answers.

title: Informational Interviews: How to Ask, What to Say, Follow Up
excerpt: Learn to request and run an informational interview: outreach email, smart questions, conversation tips and a follow-up that builds the relationship.
seo_title: Informational Interviews: How to Ask and What to Say
seo_description: Set up and run an informational interview: outreach email template, thoughtful questions, conversation tips and a thank-you follow-up that builds relationships.
content:
An informational interview is a short, friendly conversation in which you ask someone about their career to learn, get advice and build a professional relationship. To set one up, send a brief, specific message asking for 15 to 20 minutes, prepare thoughtful questions, listen more than you talk, and send a thank-you note afterward.

It is one of the most useful tools for career exploration, because it gives you information you cannot find in job postings: what the work feels like, what skills truly matter and how people entered the field. It is also a gentle form of networking, since you are asking for advice, not a favor that puts someone in an awkward position.

## Why informational interviews work

- **You learn the real picture.** Job titles hide a lot. A conversation shows daily tasks and trade-offs.
- **You discover hidden paths.** People describe routes into a field you might not have considered.
- **You build relationships.** Many people remember those who showed genuine curiosity.
- **You practice talking about yourself.** Each conversation sharpens your story.
- **You get better leads.** People may suggest others to talk to or mention opportunities.

## Step 1: Decide what you want to learn

Pick a goal. Examples: "Understand what a product analyst does day to day," "Learn how people move from teaching to training roles," or "Find out which skills matter most for entry-level marketing." A clear goal makes outreach and questions much sharper.

## Step 2: Find the right people

Start with those most likely to respond:

- Alumni from your school or program
- People in your extended network or friends of friends
- Former colleagues who changed fields
- Speakers or authors you admire
- Members of professional associations or online communities

Aim for people a few steps ahead of you, since they remember the early stages well. You do not need senior executives.

## Step 3: Send a respectful request

Keep your message short, specific and flexible.

```
Subject: Question about your path into [field]

Hi [Name],

I'm [your name], a [student/professional] interested in [field]. I found your profile through [source] and was interested in your move from [previous role] to [current role].

I'm trying to understand what the work looks like day to day and which skills matter most for newcomers. Would you be open to a 15-minute chat in the next few weeks, or to answering a couple of questions by email? I'm happy to work around your schedule.

Thank you for considering it,
[Name]
```

If they do not reply, one polite follow-up after a week or two is fine. Then move on.

## Step 4: Prepare before the conversation

Research the person and their organization. Read their profile, any articles they wrote and recent news about their company. Prepare six to eight questions and choose your top three in case time is short. Plan a 30-second introduction about yourself. Test your technology if the meeting is a video call.

## Step 5: Questions you can ask

### About their path
- How did you get into this field?
- What did you do before this role?
- What surprised you when you started?

### About the work
- What does a typical week look like?
- Which tasks take most of your time?
- What do you enjoy most, and what is most challenging?

### About skills and entry
- Which skills matter most for beginners?
- What would you recommend I learn or build first?
- How do people usually stand out when applying?

### About the field
- How is the industry changing?
- What do you wish people knew before entering?

### About next steps
- Is there anyone else you suggest I speak with?
- Is there anything I should read or do to prepare?

Avoid questions you could answer with a quick search, and avoid asking for a job.

## Step 6: Run the conversation well

- **Be on time and respect the time limit.** Offer to finish at the agreed time.
- **Start with thanks.** Briefly restate your goal.
- **Listen actively.** Take notes and ask follow-up questions.
- **Share your own story briefly.** Reciprocity makes the talk more natural.
- **Close with gratitude.** Ask whether you may stay in touch.

If the person offers to help, accept graciously, but do not push. Let them lead.

## Step 7: Follow up

Send a thank-you message within a day. Mention a specific piece of advice and what you plan to do.

```
Hi [Name],

Thank you for speaking with me today. Your advice about [specific tip] was especially useful, and I'm going to [action]. I'll share how it goes if you're interested.

Best wishes,
[Name]
```

A few weeks later, send a short update about something you did because of their advice. This closes the loop and builds goodwill.

## Keep records

Maintain a simple spreadsheet: name, role, date, key advice, next steps and follow-up date. After several conversations, patterns will emerge about skills, entry routes and employers, and you will see which direction suits you.

## Use AI to prepare, not to replace curiosity

> I am a [background] exploring a move into [field]. Draft ten questions for an informational interview with a [role] at a [type of company]. Group them into path, daily work, skills and advice. Make the questions open-ended and specific, and avoid anything I could find on a quick web search.

Edit the questions to fit the person, and read their public work first.

## A closing thought on generosity

People remember how you made them feel in a conversation. Be curious, grateful and respectful of their time, and look for small ways to give back, such as sharing a useful article or thanking them publicly when appropriate. Over months and years, these small gestures build a network that supports you throughout your career.

## Common mistakes

- **Asking for a job.** It changes the tone and can make people defensive.
- **Not preparing.** Wasting someone's time hurts your reputation.
- **Talking too much.** Keep the focus on them.
- **Going over time.** Respect the agreed length.
- **Skipping the follow-up.** Gratitude and updates make you memorable.
- **Contacting only senior leaders.** Peers and near-peers often give the best practical advice.
- **Giving up after silence.** Many people are busy. Try others.

## Next steps

Choose three people to contact this week and send each a tailored request. Prepare your own introduction using our [careers prompts](/prompts/category/careers), and keep your resume ready with the [resume builder](/resume-builder) in case they ask to see it. More guides are in the [blog](/blog).

faq.q: What is an informational interview?
faq.a: It is a short conversation, usually 15 to 30 minutes, where you ask someone about their career, role or industry to learn and seek advice. It is not a job interview, and you should not ask for a job.

faq.q: How do I ask for an informational interview?
faq.a: Send a short, polite message explaining who you are, why you chose them, and asking for a brief conversation or a few written answers. Make it easy to say yes or no, and be flexible about timing.

faq.q: What questions should I ask in an informational interview?
faq.a: Ask about their path, daily tasks, skills that matter, challenges, how the field is changing and advice for beginners. Prepare six to eight questions, but let the conversation flow naturally.

faq.q: Should I ask for a job at the end?
faq.a: No. Ask for advice instead, such as which skills to build or who else to talk to. If they know of an opening, they may mention it, and good relationships often lead to opportunities over time.

title: Skill Gap Analysis: A Simple Plan for Career Growth
excerpt: Run a skill gap analysis to compare your skills with your target role, rank the gaps and build a realistic learning plan with projects that prove your progress.
seo_title: Skill Gap Analysis: A Simple Plan for Career Growth
seo_description: Do a skill gap analysis: compare your skills with job requirements, rank gaps, choose learning methods and build a 90-day plan with proof of progress.
content:
A skill gap analysis compares what you can do today with what your target role requires, so you can see exactly what to learn next. To do one, gather real job requirements, list and rate your current skills, rank the gaps by importance, choose a learning method for each, and build a short plan that ends with proof you can show an employer.

Without a plan, career development turns into random courses and half-finished tutorials. A skill gap analysis replaces that with a focused list. It also reveals that you may be closer to your goal than you think.

## Step 1: Define your target

Choose a specific role or level. "A better job" is too vague. "Entry-level data analyst," "marketing coordinator" or "senior project manager" gives you something to measure against. If you are considering several options, run the analysis for each and compare the gaps.

## Step 2: Collect the requirements

Gather real information:

- Read ten to twenty job postings for the role. Copy the required and preferred skills into a document.
- Group similar items together, such as "spreadsheet analysis" and "data cleaning."
- Count how often each skill appears. Frequent items are core, and rare ones are bonus.
- Talk with people in the role and ask what skills matter most in practice.
- Check official or professional sources for standard competencies.

Postings sometimes list wishes instead of true requirements, so use patterns, not individual ads.

## Step 3: Inventory your current skills

List everything relevant, including skills gained outside work. Divide them into:

- **Technical skills:** tools, software, methods, languages
- **Professional skills:** communication, planning, writing, presenting, teamwork
- **Domain knowledge:** industry or subject understanding
- **Evidence:** projects, results or experience that prove each skill

For each skill, write a short example of when you used it. If you cannot give an example, your skill may be weaker than you think.

## Step 4: Rate and compare

Build a table with required skills in the first column and your honest rating in the next.

| Skill | Importance (1-5) | My level (0-5) | Gap | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Spreadsheet analysis | 5 | 3 | 2 | Budget project |
| Data visualization | 4 | 1 | 3 | None yet |
| Presenting results | 4 | 3 | 1 | Class presentation |
| SQL basics | 4 | 0 | 4 | None yet |

Calculate the gap as importance multiplied by the difference between the importance and your level, or simply focus on skills with high importance and a large distance. Ask a trusted colleague or mentor to review your ratings, since people often over- or underestimate themselves.

## Step 5: Prioritize

You cannot learn everything at once. Choose the top three gaps using these criteria:

1. **Frequency:** Does it appear in most postings?
2. **Impact:** Will it significantly improve your chances?
3. **Foundation:** Does it unlock other skills?
4. **Effort:** Can you make visible progress in a few weeks?

Delay lower-priority items. Also note strengths you can leverage, since you may already stand out in some areas.

## Step 6: Choose learning methods

Match the method to the skill:

- **Technical skills:** structured courses, tutorials and practice projects
- **Communication skills:** presenting to friends, joining clubs, writing regularly and asking for feedback
- **Domain knowledge:** books, articles, industry newsletters and conversations with practitioners
- **Leadership skills:** volunteering to coordinate small efforts and seeking mentoring
- **On-the-job learning:** asking for stretch assignments or shadowing colleagues

Whichever you choose, aim to apply what you learn quickly. Learning plus practice beats passive watching.

## Step 7: Build a 90-day plan

Create a plan with weekly steps and visible outputs.

```
Goal: Move from [current level] to [target level] in [skill] by [date].

Month 1: Learn fundamentals
- Complete [course/resource]
- Practice [number] hours per week
- Output: [small exercise or summary]

Month 2: Apply
- Build [project] using the skill
- Ask [person] for feedback
- Output: [project draft]

Month 3: Prove
- Finalize and publish [project/case study]
- Update resume and LinkedIn
- Practice explaining the work in an interview
```

Schedule specific times in your calendar. You can use the [study planner](/study-planner) to organize weekly learning blocks around your job or classes.

## Step 8: Create proof

Skills become real to employers when they are visible. Turn your learning into:

- A small project with a short write-up
- A before-and-after example
- A presentation or tutorial you created
- A contribution to a real task at work
- A concise line on your resume describing what you built and used

Be honest about your level. "Basic" or "working knowledge" is acceptable when true.

## Step 9: Review and adjust

Every month, compare your table to the original. Update ratings, remove completed gaps and add new ones. Reassess after reading new job postings, because the market changes. Ask for feedback from mentors or managers on whether your plan reflects their view.

## Use AI to organize, with caution

> Here are the requirements I collected from job postings for [role]: [paste]. Here are my current skills: [paste]. Create a gap table with importance, my level and suggested priority. Then propose a 90-day learning plan with project ideas. Point out any requirements that seem unusual or optional.

AI may misjudge your level or what employers want, so verify against actual postings and real people.

## Soft skills and how to assess them

Technical gaps are easy to list, but communication, collaboration and judgment often decide who gets hired or promoted. To assess them, ask people who have worked with you for specific feedback: "When I presented last month, what could I have made clearer?" or "How do I handle disagreement in meetings?" Look for repeated themes. Then pick one behavior to practice, such as writing shorter updates or asking clarifying questions before starting a task.

### Avoiding the perfectionism trap
Some people delay applying until every gap is closed. Most roles are filled by candidates who meet many, not all, requirements. If you meet the core requirements and can show a plan to grow in the rest, apply. Learning on the job is normal.

## Common mistakes

- **Learning everything.** Choose a few skills and go deep.
- **Collecting certificates without practice.** Employers want evidence.
- **Rating yourself dishonestly.** Accuracy helps you plan.
- **Ignoring soft skills.** Communication and teamwork are often decisive.
- **Not setting deadlines.** Open-ended plans fade.
- **Following trends blindly.** Choose skills that fit your goals.
- **Forgetting to update your resume.** Show new skills once you can prove them.

## Next steps

Collect ten job postings today and build your first gap table. Then update your materials with the [resume builder](/resume-builder) and check keyword alignment using the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker). The [careers prompts](/prompts/category/careers) include ideas for planning and practice.

faq.q: What is a skill gap analysis?
faq.a: It is a comparison between the skills you have and the skills your target role requires. The differences show what to learn first. It helps you plan your development instead of guessing or trying to learn everything.

faq.q: How do I find out which skills a job requires?
faq.a: Read ten to twenty job postings for your target role, note the repeated requirements, and talk to people who do the job. Skills that appear often are likely essential, while rare ones are usually optional.

faq.q: How long does it take to close a skill gap?
faq.a: It depends on the skill, your starting point and how much time you can practice. Some gaps close in weeks; others take months. Set small milestones and measure progress through real projects rather than hours spent.

faq.q: Do I need certificates to prove a new skill?
faq.a: Not always. Certificates can help, but employers often value evidence such as projects, work samples and clear explanations of what you did. Combine credentials with practical proof when possible. Choose proof that matches the role.

title: Video and Phone Interview Tips: Setup, Delivery and Etiquette
excerpt: Prepare for video and phone interviews with practical tips on technology, lighting, eye contact, voice and etiquette, plus a checklist to run before every call.
seo_title: Video and Phone Interview Tips: Setup and Etiquette
seo_description: Ace video and phone interviews with tips on tech setup, lighting, eye contact, voice, note use and etiquette, plus a pre-call checklist and backup plans.
content:
To do well in a video or phone interview, test your technology early, choose a quiet and well-lit space, speak clearly with a steady pace, and keep the same preparation you would use for an in-person meeting. The medium changes the delivery, not the substance: employers still want clear, specific answers and signs that you are easy to work with.

Remote interviews are common, and they have their own challenges: delays, distractions and the lack of body language. A little preparation removes most of the stress.

## Before the interview

### Confirm the details
Check the date, time and time zone, the platform, the interviewer names and whether you need to install software. Add the link to your calendar, and save a phone number to call if something goes wrong.

### Test your technology
- Try the platform in advance and update the app if needed
- Check your camera, microphone and speakers or headphones
- Test your internet connection and connect with a cable if possible
- Charge your device or plug it in
- Close unnecessary programs and silence notifications

### Prepare your space
- Choose a quiet room and tell others you will be busy
- Place light in front of you, such as a window or a lamp behind the camera
- Use a tidy, neutral background
- Position the camera at eye level by stacking books or using a stand
- Sit on a stable chair with good posture

### Dress professionally
Dress as you would for an in-person interview, from head to toe. It helps your mindset, and it avoids surprises if you need to stand up. Avoid busy patterns that look distracting on camera.

## Video interview delivery

### Eye contact and posture
Look at the camera when you speak, which feels like eye contact to the viewer. When listening, you can glance at the screen. Sit upright, keep your hands visible when gesturing, and smile naturally.

### Voice and pacing
Slight delays are common on calls. Pause briefly before answering, and avoid interrupting. Speak a little slower than normal and with clear articulation. If audio breaks, politely ask the person to repeat.

### Using notes
Place a short list near your camera: key achievements, stories, questions for them and the names of interviewers. Do not read from it. A few reminders are enough to keep you on track.

### Screen sharing and tools
If you may be asked to share your screen or complete a task, practice beforehand. Close personal tabs and notifications, and have documents ready in a tidy folder.

## Phone interview delivery

Phone interviews depend entirely on your voice.

- Take the call in a quiet place with strong reception
- Use headphones or a stable phone stand so your hands are free
- Stand or sit upright, which tends to improve your voice
- Smile while talking, which comes across in tone
- Keep your resume, job description and notes in front of you
- Use verbal signposts like "There are three parts to my answer" to help the listener follow

Because the interviewer cannot see your reactions, show you are listening with short, natural acknowledgments, and avoid long silences.

## Opening and closing

Start with a friendly greeting, thank them for their time and be ready for small talk. At the end, restate your interest in the role, ask about the next steps and thank them again. Send a follow-up email within a day.

## Common remote interview formats

- **One-way recorded interviews:** You record answers to set questions with a time limit. Practice speaking to a camera, and structure each answer with the STAR method.
- **Panel video calls:** Look at the camera, address the person who asked the question, and include others with brief glances.
- **Technical or case sessions:** Think aloud, ask clarifying questions and explain your reasoning.

## A pre-interview checklist

```
[ ] Time zone and link confirmed
[ ] Platform tested, updated
[ ] Camera, mic, headphones working
[ ] Charger plugged in, notifications off
[ ] Quiet space, lighting checked
[ ] Neutral background, camera at eye level
[ ] Resume, job description, notes ready
[ ] Water within reach
[ ] Backup phone number and hotspot
[ ] Three questions prepared for the interviewer
```

## Practice with AI and a friend

> Act as an interviewer on a video call for a [job title] role. Ask me one question at a time. After each of my typed answers, give feedback on structure, clarity and length. Also remind me about voice and pacing tips for video interviews, and ask me a follow-up.

Then practice aloud, record yourself on camera and review your posture, eye contact and speech speed. A friend can add feedback on how you appear and sound.

## Handling problems gracefully

- **Connection drops:** Rejoin quickly, then apologize briefly and continue.
- **Distractions:** Stay calm if a pet or noise intrudes, apologize and move on.
- **Blank mind:** Pause, take a sip of water and ask to repeat the question.
- **Awkward silence due to delay:** Wait a beat before answering to avoid talking over the interviewer.

## Accessibility and personal circumstances

Not everyone has a perfect home setup, and that is acceptable. If your space is shared, tell the interviewer briefly and calmly at the start, or ask to reschedule if you need a quieter time. If you need accommodations, such as captions, extra time or a different format, you can request them in advance, and the employer should be able to explain the options. Use a virtual background only if it looks clean and does not distract; a tidy real background is often better.

### Energy management
Interviews are tiring, especially several in a row. Drink water, take a short walk beforehand, and leave a few minutes between calls to reset. Write the name and role of each interviewer on a sticky note so you can address them correctly.

### Making a human connection through a screen
Remote interviews can feel flat, so work to create warmth. Greet the interviewer by name, nod while they speak, and use a friendly tone. Refer back to something they said earlier, such as a project or challenge, so the conversation feels collaborative. A genuine, relaxed manner often matters as much as a perfect answer.

## Common mistakes

- **Skipping the tech test.** Most issues are preventable.
- **Poor lighting.** Dark or backlit video makes you hard to see.
- **Looking at yourself.** Hide self-view if it distracts you.
- **Multitasking.** Close other apps and stay focused.
- **Reading a script.** It sounds unnatural.
- **Interrupting because of lag.** Pause first.
- **Forgetting to follow up.** A thank-you note matters.

## Next steps

Run a full mock interview using your actual setup this week. Practice answers with the [careers prompt library](/prompts/category/careers), and make sure your documents are ready with the [resume builder](/resume-builder) and [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder).

faq.q: How early should I join a video interview?
faq.a: Log in five to ten minutes early to test your connection, audio and camera. Stay in the waiting room or on the page until you are admitted, and avoid joining too early if the interviewer is mid-meeting.

faq.q: Can I use notes during a phone or video interview?
faq.a: Yes, brief notes are fine and often helpful, such as key points, questions and your stories. Avoid reading long scripts, and keep eye contact with the camera or focus on listening during phone calls.

faq.q: Where should I look during a video interview?
faq.a: Look at the camera when you speak to create eye contact, and glance at the screen when listening. Place the interviewer window near the camera so your gaze does not drift too far.

faq.q: What if technology fails during the interview?
faq.a: Stay calm, tell the interviewer, and try to reconnect. Have a phone number and a backup plan, such as a mobile hotspot or an alternative device. Most interviewers understand technical problems.

title: A Weekly Job Search System: Routine, Tracker and Goals
excerpt: Turn a stressful job hunt into a manageable routine with weekly goals, a simple tracker, time blocks and review habits that keep your search moving.
seo_title: A Weekly Job Search System: Routine and Tracker
seo_description: Organize your job search with a weekly routine, a simple tracker, realistic goals and review habits that keep you consistent and reduce stress during the hunt.
content:
The best job searches run on a simple weekly system: set measurable goals, block time for specific activities, track every application and contact in one place, and review what is working each week. A routine reduces anxiety, prevents missed follow-ups and helps you improve instead of repeating the same approach.

Job hunting can feel endless because there is no obvious finish line each day. A system creates small finish lines, so you can feel progress even before the offer arrives.

## The four activities of a job search

Think of your search as four types of work:

1. **Preparing:** resume, profile, portfolio, stories
2. **Finding and applying:** searching, tailoring and submitting
3. **Connecting:** networking, informational chats, follow-ups
4. **Growing:** interview practice, learning skills

Many people spend all their time on applying. A balanced week includes all four, because applications alone have a low success rate for many roles, and the other activities strengthen every application.

## Step 1: Set your target

Write a one-paragraph description of your search:

- Target roles (two or three titles)
- Preferred industries or company types
- Location or remote requirements
- Minimum requirements for pay, schedule and growth
- Timeline and any constraints

A clear target prevents you from drifting toward every posting and helps you decide quickly what to skip.

## Step 2: Create a simple tracker

A spreadsheet with these columns is enough:

| Column | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Company | Who you applied to |
| Role and link | Remember the posting |
| Date applied | Plan follow-ups |
| Resume/cover version | Know what you sent |
| Contact | Recruiter or referrer |
| Status | Saved, applied, screening, interview, offer, closed |
| Next action | What you will do next |
| Next action date | Prevents forgetting |
| Notes | Interview questions, impressions |

Add a second tab for networking: name, relationship, date contacted, response and follow-up. Update it at the end of each day.

## Step 3: Plan your week

Divide your time into blocks. A sample structure for a full-time search:

- **Monday:** Review tracker, set goals, search and shortlist roles
- **Tuesday:** Tailor and submit applications
- **Wednesday:** Networking messages and informational chats
- **Thursday:** Interview practice and skill building
- **Friday:** Applications, follow-ups and weekly review

If you are employed, compress this into short blocks of 30 to 60 minutes on several days. Use a planner or the [study planner](/study-planner) to schedule blocks like appointments.

## Step 4: Set realistic weekly goals

Use goals that you control (inputs), not just results (outputs). Examples:

```
This week:
- Submit 6 tailored applications
- Send 5 networking messages
- Have 1 informational conversation
- Practice 3 interview answers aloud
- Spend 2 hours on one skill or project
- Follow up on 3 older applications
```

Adjust numbers to your time and energy. It is better to hit a modest target consistently than to set an impossible one.

## Step 5: Apply with focus

Before applying, check how well the job matches your skills. If you match most of the core requirements, tailor your resume and submit. Save time with a master resume and a library of reusable bullet points. Use the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) to compare your resume to a posting. Do not apply to roles that clearly do not fit, since it wastes effort and may harm your sense of progress.

## Step 6: Follow up on schedule

Set follow-up dates when you apply. If you do not hear back within the stated period, send a short, polite message. After interviews, send a thank-you within a day. A tracker with next action dates makes this easy.

## Step 7: Review weekly

On Friday, spend 20 minutes reflecting:

- What did I complete compared to my goals?
- Which activities led to responses or conversations?
- What questions did I struggle with in interviews?
- Which applications or messages should I adjust?
- What will I change next week?

Look for patterns. If you apply a lot but get few interviews, improve your resume or targeting. If you get interviews but no offers, invest in practice and storytelling. If you get no replies to messages, refine your outreach.

## Step 8: Protect your energy

Job searching is emotionally demanding. Protect yourself:

- Keep a regular sleep and exercise routine
- Set a daily stopping time
- Take real breaks and spend time with friends
- Celebrate small wins, such as a good conversation
- Ask for support if the stress feels heavy

Rejection is part of the process and does not define your worth.

## Use AI to organize the work

> I am searching for [role] jobs and can spend [hours] per week. Create a weekly schedule with specific tasks for applications, networking, interview practice and learning. Include a short Friday review checklist and three questions I should ask myself when results are slow.

Adapt it to your situation, and keep human contact central.

## Adjusting the system to your situation

### If you are still employed
Protect your current job by searching outside work hours and using personal devices and accounts. Schedule interviews at the beginning or end of the day when possible, and avoid discussing your search with colleagues until you are ready. Fewer, higher-quality applications often work better than large numbers when time is limited.

### If you are a student or recent graduate
Align your system with your academic calendar. Use quieter weeks for applications and networking, and reserve exam periods for lighter tasks like updating your tracker. Career services, alumni groups and professors are valuable allies, so make them a regular part of your week.

### If your search is taking longer than expected
After several weeks, review your target. Are your requirements realistic for your market? Would adjacent roles or smaller companies be worth considering? Ask a mentor to review your resume and interview answers. Sometimes a small adjustment, such as changing your headline or practicing one weak answer, makes a visible difference.

## Common mistakes

- **Applying without tracking.** You will lose track of follow-ups.
- **Mass applying with one resume.** Tailor your top sections.
- **Only using job boards.** Combine them with networking.
- **Ignoring rejection patterns.** Use them as information.
- **Working without breaks.** Burnout hurts performance.
- **Not preparing for interviews until invited.** Practice early.
- **Quitting a routine after a few rejections.** Consistency wins over time.

## Next steps

Create your tracker and schedule next week's blocks today. Prepare your documents with the [resume builder](/resume-builder), and use the [careers prompts](/prompts/category/careers) for interview and networking practice. More step-by-step job search guides are in the [blog](/blog).

faq.q: How many hours a week should I spend on job searching?
faq.a: If you are unemployed, many people find that 15 to 25 focused hours works well. If you are employed, a few hours each week may be realistic. Consistency and quality matter more than raw hours.

faq.q: How many jobs should I apply to each week?
faq.a: There is no perfect number. Set a target you can sustain, such as five to ten tailored applications, and balance it with networking and skill building. Tailored applications usually beat mass applying.

faq.q: What should a job search tracker include?
faq.a: Include company, role, link, date applied, contact person, resume version, status, next action and notes. A spreadsheet or notes app works. The key is updating it regularly and acting on follow-up dates.

faq.q: How do I stay motivated during a long job search?
faq.a: Break the process into small weekly goals, track progress, celebrate small wins, take breaks and talk with friends or mentors. Keeping a routine and caring for your health helps you stay resilient.

title: How to Ask for a Promotion or Raise: Prepare, Pitch, Follow Up
excerpt: Prepare a strong case for a promotion or raise: track your impact, understand expectations, choose the right moment and use a clear script and follow-up plan.
seo_title: How to Ask for a Promotion or Raise at Work
seo_description: Ask for a promotion or raise with confidence: document your impact, research the market, time the talk, use a simple script and plan for any answer you receive.
content:
To ask for a promotion or raise, build a short evidence-based case showing the results you have delivered and the responsibilities you now carry, research market pay for your role, request a dedicated meeting with your manager, present your case calmly, and agree on next steps. Preparation matters far more than confidence alone.

Many people wait for their work to speak for itself, but managers are busy and may not see everything you do. Asking is a normal part of career growth when it is done with preparation and respect.

## Step 1: Understand how promotions work at your company

Every organization differs. Find out:

- Is there a formal promotion process, and when does it happen?
- What are the criteria for the next level?
- Who decides, and who influences the decision?
- Are there review cycles for pay?
- What did recent promotions look like?

Read any job level guides or competency frameworks. If none exist, ask your manager: "What would I need to demonstrate to be considered for the next level?"

## Step 2: Check whether you are operating at the next level

A promotion usually recognizes work you already do, not work you hope to do. Ask yourself:

- Am I handling responsibilities beyond my current job description?
- Do others come to me for guidance?
- Am I delivering consistent results over time?
- Am I leading or influencing, not only completing tasks?

If you find gaps, discuss a development plan with your manager first. That conversation can be the foundation for a later request.

## Step 3: Build your evidence file

Track your accomplishments throughout the year. Keep a running document with:

- Projects completed and their outcomes
- Problems you solved
- Positive feedback from colleagues, customers or managers
- New responsibilities you took on
- Skills you developed
- Ways you saved time, improved quality or helped others

Use numbers only when accurate. Otherwise, describe outcomes clearly: "Redesigned the onboarding checklist, and new team members now start tasks a week earlier," if that is true. Choose the top three to five items that best support your case.

## Step 4: Research your market value

For a raise, compare your pay to similar roles using salary surveys, job postings with pay ranges and professional contacts. Account for location, company size and experience. Be realistic, and prepare a reasonable range. This is general information, and local rules and company policies vary.

## Step 5: Choose the right time and format

- Schedule a dedicated meeting instead of raising it in passing. Say, "I'd like to discuss my growth and compensation. Could we find 30 minutes this week?"
- Pick a calm moment, ideally after a success or before budget planning.
- Avoid asking during layoffs, crises or when your manager is under heavy pressure.
- Prefer a private conversation, in person or on video.

## Step 6: Present your case

Use a simple structure:

1. **Appreciation:** Thank your manager for support and opportunities.
2. **Results:** Share your top achievements and added responsibilities.
3. **Ask:** State clearly what you are requesting, whether a title change, raise or both.
4. **Rationale:** Explain how it reflects your contribution and market range.
5. **Question:** Ask for their view and next steps.

### Script
```
Thank you for making time. I've enjoyed working on [projects] over the past [period]. Since [date], I've taken on [new responsibilities] and delivered [results]. Based on this and what I see for similar roles, I'd like to discuss moving to [title] and adjusting my compensation to [figure or range]. I'd appreciate your thoughts and what steps we can take to make that happen.
```

After you ask, stop and listen. Avoid apologizing or filling silence.

## Step 7: Handle each response

### If they say yes
Thank them and ask when it takes effect. Request written confirmation of the new title and terms.

### If they need time
Ask when you may expect an answer and offer to provide supporting information. Follow up politely if the date passes.

### If they say not now
Ask:
- What specifically would I need to do or show?
- What is a realistic timeline to revisit this?
- Can we agree on goals and a check-in date?

Write a summary email afterward: "Thank you for our conversation. To confirm, we agreed that I will focus on A and B, and we will review in [month]."

### If the answer is a firm no
Consider why. Is it budget, performance, timing or fit? Decide whether to continue, develop in another way or explore opportunities elsewhere. Stay professional either way.

## Step 8: Follow up and keep delivering

Whatever the outcome, send a thank-you note. Keep documenting results, and meet agreed goals. If a deadline passes, request a follow-up meeting with updated evidence.

## Use AI to prepare your pitch

> Here is a list of my achievements and responsibilities over the past year: [paste]. Help me turn them into a concise three-minute case for a promotion to [title], with three bullet points of evidence and a calm closing question. Do not add facts or numbers I have not provided.

Rehearse out loud, and adjust the language to sound like you.

## If you work in a flat or small organization

Not every workplace has formal levels. In a small company, the path may involve expanding your scope, owning a new area or being named lead of a project. Frame your request around the value you create and the responsibilities you want to take on. Ask what the business needs next and how you can fill that need, and suggest a title or pay review that reflects the added scope.

### Building your case between reviews
Do not wait for a once-a-year meeting. Share short updates with your manager regularly, ask for feedback each quarter and make your goals known: "I would like to grow into a lead role within the next year. What should I focus on?" This turns the eventual request into a natural step rather than a surprise.

### Staying positive while you wait
Even when the answer is delayed, keep your performance steady. Continue learning, support your teammates and avoid complaining. A reputation for reliability and growth is valuable whether you stay or move on.

## Common mistakes

- **Making it about personal expenses.** Focus on contribution and market value.
- **Giving ultimatums.** Threats damage trust.
- **Comparing yourself to colleagues.** Stick to your own results.
- **Arriving without evidence.** Prepare specifics.
- **Waiting too long.** Do not assume your manager knows your goals.
- **Asking at the wrong time.** Timing influences outcomes.
- **Getting defensive after a no.** Ask questions and plan next steps.

## Next steps

Start your evidence file today, and update your resume with the [resume builder](/resume-builder) to keep your achievements ready. For wording ideas and practice, use the [careers prompt collection](/prompts/category/careers), and browse more growth guides in the [blog](/blog).

faq.q: When is the best time to ask for a promotion?
faq.a: Good times include after a major success, during performance review cycles, when you have taken on larger responsibilities, or when budgets are being planned. Avoid periods of company stress or when your manager is overwhelmed.

faq.q: How do I prove I deserve a raise?
faq.a: Document specific achievements, added responsibilities and measurable impact, and compare your pay to market data for similar roles. Present your case calmly, focusing on the value you provide rather than personal needs.

faq.q: What if my manager says no?
faq.a: Ask what would need to change and when it can be reconsidered. Request specific goals and a timeline, and follow up in writing. A no for now can still produce a plan, and it may help you decide whether to look elsewhere.

faq.q: Should I ask for a title change or a raise first?
faq.a: It depends on what matters to you. Ideally ask for both when your responsibilities have grown. If budgets are tight, a title or scope increase now with a pay review later can be a reasonable compromise.
